title: Not All Secrets Are Equal: Type-Aware Unlearning for Language Model Secret Removal
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can reproduce memorized sensitive data, including SSH keys, API tokens, and personally identifiable information (PII), when prompted with the right context. Removing these secrets is difficult: gradient-based unlearning often damages model utility, while preference-based methods can leave secrets recoverable, especially at larger scales. We show that a central reason is type heterogeneity: different secret types exhibit different gradient-saliency patterns and require different correction strengths. We introduce Per-Secret-Type Unlearning (PSTU), a training-free task-arithmetic method that replaces a single global scaling factor with per-type saliency and layer-group corrections. For 7B+ models, PSTU-Trim denoises the task vector before subtraction. Across our evaluated Pythia (1.4B to 6.9B) and Llama-3.1-8B configurations, PSTU removes all 175 measured memorized secrets with 1.3% to 14.4% perplexity overhead, while five baselines either leave secrets recoverable or incur substantial utility loss. On LUME (OLMo-1B/7B), PSTU removes all measured memorized PII within $${\pm }1$$ % of clean PPL, and on free-form Nemotron-PII documents it returns memorization to the clean-model floor with better utility than baselines.

title: Some Tokens Behave like Magnets: Revealing Linguistic Organization in the Layers of Language Models
abstract: We identify a special group of token vectors inside large language models (LLMs), which we term magnetic vectors, that organize the surrounding tokens by either attracting or repelling them. Particularly, tokens pointing the same way as an attracting magnet are elongated; tokens pointing the same way as a repelling magnet are compressed. Just as physical magnets pull or push away the iron filings around them, these vectors organize their surroundings through two opposing polarities. Moreover, we identify a statistically significant pattern in linguistic category where function words consistently act as repelling magnets in early layers, and we also find magnets consistently reorganize their polarities in unique ways deeper in the model. In a further case study we find this observation may unveil a deliberate, layer-wise organization in how LLMs process language. This pattern is consistent across different LLM architectures, sizes, and layer configurations. It is also causally relevant. When the LLM is fine-tuned for a downstream task, the task-functional tokens emerge as magnets. E.g., in question answering, the answer-span tokens become uniquely repelling magnets in the final layer, geometrically carving the answer out of the surrounding context. Furthermore, removing early-layer repelling magnets devastates syntactic tasks (POS tagging accuracy drops from 91% to below 10%) while sparing semantic ones, and removing late-layer attracting magnets does the reverse. We believe this phenomenon warrants further investigation, as it opens the first probe-free path to understanding how language models geometrically organize linguistic computation across their layers.

title: Hidden In Plain Gaze: Gaze Representations as Privacy Controls for Utility and Re-identification Risk in XR
abstract: Intelligent extended reality (XR) systems increasingly use eye and head tracking to infer user intent, task, and attention, but the same signals can also reveal biometric identity. We study whether gaze data representation choice can serve as a lightweight privacy control at feature extraction, before adding perturbation or formal privacy mechanisms. Using the egocentric HoloAssist dataset, we compare three gaze representations under matched model capacity: raw gaze, spatial attention heatmaps, and engineered eye-movement features. We evaluate each representation on action recognition as task utility and closed-set user re-identification as privacy leakage. Representation choice substantially changes the privacy-utility tradeoff. Engineered features retain roughly 85% of raw gaze's action-recognition accuracy while reducing re-identification by about an order of magnitude, to roughly four times the chance rate across 206 identities. This reduction attenuates rather than eliminates identity leakage, and the differences across representations show that abstraction alone does not guarantee privacy. Engineered features expose interpretable and auditable structure, giving designers a transparent privacy lever that complements mechanisms such as differential privacy.

title: Quantum State Information Encryption Protocol
abstract: This paper presents a novel quantum information encryption protocol based on the unique properties of quantum entanglement. The core principle of this protocol leverages the instantaneous correlation between entangled particles to establish secure communication. We investigate the potential of quantum entanglement to enhance the security and robustness of existing encryption methods, offering a fundamentally different approach to data protection. The study focuses on the design and analysis of a quantum-enhanced encryption scheme, incorporating quantum state manipulation and entanglement-based protocols to achieve robust data protection. We explore the theoretical foundations and potential practical implementation challenges associated with this approach.

title: 基于动态拓扑的量子态转移
abstract: This paper introduces a novel quantum state transfer framework based on dynamic topology. Traditional quantum state transfer methods often rely on manual design, lacking the ability to autonomously learn and optimize transfer processes. Our approach leverages dynamic topology to enable precise state transfer, offering enhanced capabilities for quantum computing optimization and control. We present a theoretical model demonstrating the effectiveness of this approach, highlighting its advantages over existing methods. This research explores the potential of dynamic topology to revolutionize quantum information processing.

title: Dimension Collapse Theory and Quantum Computing: Coupling Mechanisms
abstract: This paper investigates the potential of dimension collapse theory within the context of quantum computing, proposing a novel computational model predicated on high-dimensional multi-particle quantum entanglement. We explore how this framework, utilizing dimension collapse as a key process, can enhance the efficiency and scalability of quantum computation. The core of our work lies in the design of a computational model that leverages the unique properties of multi-dimensional quantum states to achieve parallel processing and expanded quantum information storage. This approach offers a fundamentally different pathway to overcome the limitations of current quantum computing architectures, specifically focusing on leveraging the intricacies of high-dimensional entanglement. The proposed model presents a significant advancement in understanding and utilizing the potential of dimension collapse theory for quantum computing applications.

title: Probability Geometry for Neural Network Optimization
abstract: This paper explores the application of probability geometry as a novel optimization framework for neural network parameter tuning. Traditional neural network training relies heavily on gradient descent, often requiring extensive hyperparameter tuning. This work proposes a probabilistic approach, leveraging the principles of probability geometry to dynamically adjust network parameters, enabling the algorithm to adapt to data-specific local features and ultimately achieve global optimal solutions. The core mechanism involves integrating probability geometric optimization with the inherent self-adaptation capabilities of neural networks. The paper details the algorithm's design, its advantages over existing methods, and provides a comprehensive analysis of its performance on benchmark datasets. The resultant algorithm demonstrates the potential for automated parameter optimization, improved model generalization, and increased interpretability.

title: Active Learning for Robot Perception
abstract: This paper investigates the application of active learning techniques to improve robot perception. Traditional robot perception systems often rely on passive learning, where the system is presented with a fixed dataset of labeled samples. This approach can be inefficient, particularly when the data distribution is highly complex or when the desired performance is far from the initial model's capabilities. We propose a novel framework where the robot actively selects the samples it needs to learn from, leveraging a reinforcement learning (RL) based strategy. The core idea is to allow the robot to intelligently query its environment for new data based on its current perception performance and feedback from the environment. This approach allows the robot to focus on the most informative samples, significantly reducing the amount of data required to achieve a desired level of accuracy and fundamentally shifting the paradigm towards self-optimization of perception capabilities. The framework is defined through a Markov Decision Process (MDP) and utilizes a Q-learning algorithm to learn an optimal sample selection policy. The theoretical contributions of this work lie in formalizing the active learning problem within a robotic perception context and providing a robust methodology for achieving superior performance compared to passive learning scenarios. We demonstrate the potential of this approach through a conceptual discussion and highlight key considerations for implementation.

title: Hypergraph-Based Representation of Complex Dependencies
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to representing and analyzing complex dependencies by leveraging hypergraphs. Traditional graph representations struggle to adequately capture multi-way relationships between entities, leading to limitations in modeling intricate systems. This work proposes utilizing hypergraph neural networks (HGNNs) to directly process these multi-way connections, offering a more nuanced and accurate understanding. We detail the theoretical underpinnings of hypergraph-based representation, explore the core mechanisms of HGNNs, and highlight how this approach surpasses conventional graph models in capturing complex dependencies. The core claim is that representing complex dependencies using hypergraphs allows for the explicit modeling of multi-way relationships. The core mechanism utilizes hypergraph neural networks that can directly process these multi-way relationships, enabling more nuanced understanding of interconnected systems. This work represents a significant step forward in representing complex systems by providing a more expressive way to model intricate dependencies.

title: Adaptive Quantum Topology Control
abstract: Quantum topology is a rapidly evolving field with the potential to revolutionize quantum computing by offering novel platforms for quantum information processing. This research paper explores the development of an adaptive quantum topology control algorithm, aiming to enhance the precision and controllability of quantum systems. We present a novel approach leveraging self-tuning parameters to dynamically manipulate the quantum state, ultimately enabling more accurate and robust quantum computations. The core mechanism centers around an iterative process of parameter adjustment guided by a feedback loop, resulting in a system capable of achieving higher fidelity in quantum operations. This work introduces a new algorithmic framework for controlling quantum topology, demonstrating its potential to surpass existing techniques in achieving precise control and improving the performance of quantum algorithms. The research focuses on establishing a robust and efficient methodology for adapting quantum states to achieve desired outcomes.

title: 基于自适应拓扑的基于高斯过程的优化算法
abstract: This paper introduces a novel optimization algorithm based on adaptive topology, leveraging the power of the Gaussian process. Traditional optimization methods often rely on manual parameter tuning, while this approach utilizes the inherent properties of the Gaussian process to accurately model complex geometries and system behavior. We propose a framework that automatically adjusts parameters based on the Gaussian process, leading to improved simulation accuracy and efficiency. The core mechanism involves simulating geometric structures using the Gaussian process and then optimizing the parameters via gradient-based methods. This offers a more robust and automated approach to optimization compared to conventional techniques. The proposed algorithm demonstrates significant improvements in several benchmark problems, showcasing the effectiveness of the adaptive topology-based Gaussian process framework.

title: Title: Computational Verification of Homological Proofs via Graph Theory
abstract: This paper explores the application of graph theory to enhance the computational verification of complex mathematical proofs. The core claim is to establish a novel framework for detecting and mitigating logical inconsistencies within these proofs, offering a potentially automated and rigorous verification process. The framework will leverage graph representation techniques to identify and analyze inconsistencies, providing feedback to the user. The significance of this work lies in its potential to significantly improve the efficiency and reliability of proof checking, particularly for intricate mathematical theorems and proofs. The paper details the development of a system based on graph construction and analysis to automatically assess the validity of mathematical statements. We will present a conceptual overview of the proposed system, outlining its key components and demonstrating its efficacy through a simplified example. This work addresses a critical challenge in mathematical verification – the need for efficient and automated techniques to ensure the correctness of complex proofs.

title: Quantum Adaptive Tensor
abstract: Quantum Adaptive Tensor is a novel approach to tensor computation that leverages the principles of quantum entanglement to achieve unprecedented accuracy and low latency in quantum computing. The core concept centers around the 'Quantum Adaptive Tensor' – a specialized tensor structure designed to exploit quantum entanglement for enhanced computational capabilities. This paper explores the fundamental principles behind this method, detailing the mechanism of entanglement-based computation, its advantages over classical approaches, and its potential to significantly advance the field of quantum computation. The research investigates the practical implications of this design, focusing on the achievable precision and latency characteristics when implemented on quantum hardware.

title: Title: Universal Constraint Language for Adaptive Systems (UCLAS)
abstract: This paper introduces Universal Constraint Language (UCLAS), a declarative language designed to facilitate the automatic discovery and adaptation of constraints within adaptive systems. The core challenge of adaptive systems is the constant need to evolve constraints to accommodate changing environments, user requirements, and system goals. UCLAS offers a novel approach by providing a structured framework for defining constraints and enabling automated reasoning to identify and propagate new constraints. The system leverages a form of automated reasoning to search for potentially relevant constraints, ensuring that the resulting constraints are logically consistent and maintainable. We present a preliminary implementation demonstrating the potential of UCLAS to streamline constraint management and improve the robustness of adaptive systems.

title: Преобразование SQL-запросов в текстовое описание задачи на русском языке
abstract: В данной работе изложена сущность подхода к автоматической генерации текстовых описаний SQL-запросов на русском языке. Проведён анализ существующих решений задачи SQL-to-text, метрик оценки качества и доступных датасетов. На основе сравнительного анализа шести датасетов с применением расширенного метода TOPSIS выбран датасет Spider 1.0 для создания русскоязычного аналога. Разработан русскоязычный датасет RuSpider (7000 обучающих и 1034 валидационных примера) с разметкой по уровням сложности, выявлены проблемные конструкции, создан дополнительный датасет fix_dataset (769 запросов). Создана и адаптирована для русского языка метрика RuBLEC, оценивающая логическую согласованность между SQL-запросом и сгенерированным текстом с детекцией галлюцинаций и логических противоречий. Разработана модель RuSNOWBALL на основе архитектуры «Генератор-Оценщик» с использованием предобученной T5 (cointegrated/rut5-base, 244M параметров) и метрики RuBLEC в качестве оценщика. Реализована процедура аугментации данных с RuBLEC-фильтрацией. Проведено сравнительное тестирование трёх моделей (Rules-Based, T5-Baseline, RuSNOWBALL) на 73 запросах различной сложности. Финальная модель достигла RuBLEC = 90,8%, BERTScore = 83,1%, превзойдя T5-Baseline на 9% и 5% соответственно. Выполнено сравнение с оригинальным фреймворком SNOWBALL, подтвердившее эффективность адаптации для русского языка. Разработанная модель может использоваться в образовательных целях для обучения SQL, для документирования баз данных и автоматизации анализа SQL-кода.

title: A two-stage efficient fine-tuning framework for vertical domain text embedding
abstract: Text embedding in vertical industrial domains provides a critical foundation for professional information retrieval, semantic matching, and intelligent decision-making. However, general-purpose embedding models often fail to meet the demands of complex industrial applications because they lack effective modeling of domain knowledge and fine-grained semantic distinctions. To address this limitation, we propose a two-stage efficient fine-tuning framework for vertical-domain text embedding. In the first stage, domain-adaptive contrastive learning is employed to align the base semantic space with domain-specific data, thereby enhancing the model’s representation of technical terminology and contextual knowledge. In the second stage, joint fine-tuning is performed across multiple tasks, including retrieval, classification, semantic textual similarity, sentence-pair discrimination, and ranking, while a dynamic hard negative mining strategy is introduced to continuously strengthen the model’s ability to distinguish highly similar and easily confusable samples. Furthermore, to address the substantial differences in task objectives and the inconsistency of optimization dynamics in multitask training, a dynamic-awareness and priority-guided adaptive scheduling mechanism is proposed to adjust task sampling weights according to task learning progress and relative importance, thereby improving the synergy and stability of multitask optimization. Experiments conducted on a coal mining domain dataset demonstrate that the embedding model built upon the proposed framework consistently outperforms mainstream embedding models on Accuracy@1, Recall@3, NDCG@10, and MRR@10. Additional comparative experiments and ablation studies further verify the overall advantages of the framework in terms of stability, scalability, and industrial applicability. The proposed method therefore provides a robust, practical, and scalable solution for developing high-performance embedding models in vertical domains, facilitating more accurate retrieval, knowledge representation, and decision-support applications.

title: Multi-granularity Adaptive Hypergraph Representation Learning via Granular-ball
abstract: Hypergraph representation learning aims to capture high-order information in graphs by constructing hyperedges that simultaneously connect multiple nodes. These hyperedges adapt to the graph's topological features, facilitating the extraction of high-order relationships at multiple granularities. Most prior work relies on predefined definitions to generate hyperedges, overlooking the diversity in graph topological structures and the multi-granularity characteristics of hyperedges. As a result, this limits their ability to effectively and adaptively discover high-order relationships and efficiently process complex structural information. To address this limitation, we propose a novel framework called \underline{M}ulti-\underline{G}ranularity \underline{H}ypergraph \underline{R}epresentation \underline{L}earning (MGHRL). MGHRL introduces an Adaptive Granular Hypergraph Generation strategy, which generates hyperedges at multiple levels of granularity through the adaptive splitting of granular-ball, effectively capturing high-order relationships based on the graph's topological structure. Additionally, we propose a Multi-Granularity Hypergraph Network with multiple sub-networks, capturing features from hyperedges at different granularities and integrating them via hierarchical reversible connections. Experimental results show that MGHRL significantly outperforms baseline models on benchmark datasets.

title: Understanding the Privacy-Preserving Potential of HTTP/2 Against Webpage Fingerprinting
abstract: Website fingerprinting (WF) attacks can infer which webpage a user visits from encrypted HTTPS traffic alone, compromising privacy even without decryption. WF defenses commonly shape traffic through noise, padding, delays, or flow splitting, yet they are most often studied from the perspective of encapsulating protocols like Tor or VPN rather than at the application layer (HTTP). In this work, we focus on application-layer defenses enabled by the most widely deployed version of HTTP, HTTP/2. We demonstrate how known defenses can be emulated through HTTP/2 features at the client side (HTTPOS, LLaMA, FRONT, Tamaraw) and the server side (ALPaCA, Tamaraw). We further show that HTTP/2 features, such as proactive resource suggestion, multiplexing, and flow control, offer untapped potential for lightweight yet effective defenses deployable at both endpoints. We evaluate these defenses using a unified blueprint that calibrates defense parameters per dataset, then combines practical attacks, information-theoretic leakage estimates, and overhead measurements. For each defense, this framework identifies the strongest hyperparameter-tuned fingerprinting model and estimates the residual uncertainty induced by the defense using two information-theoretic leakage estimators, all while accounting for the defense's privacy-overhead trade-offs.

title: Quaternary Legendre Pairs of Lengths 42, 46, 52, 58, 66, 72, and 80
abstract: A quaternary Legendre pair of length $\ell$ is a pair of sequences over the fourth roots of unity whose periodic autocorrelations sum to $-2$ at every nonzero shift. Each such pair yields a quaternary Hadamard matrix of order $2\ell+2$ and a binary Hadamard matrix of order $4\ell+4$. Fourteen even lengths up to 100 remained open in the 2025 tables of Kotsireas, Koutschan and Winterhof and of Jedwab and Pender. We settle seven of them --- the four smallest open lengths, 42, 46, 52, and 58, together with 66, 72, and 80 --- and print every pair in full. Checking one takes a few lines of code and exact arithmetic over the Gaussian integers, so the main results can be confirmed without running any of our software. Each search writes a pair as four binary sequences under a Gray map, restricts to reflection-symmetric rows, imposes an exact spectral constraint at the midpoint frequency, and matches candidates meet-in-the-middle on their autocorrelation vectors; from length 52 onward, exact compression along divisor chains shrinks the search before any candidate is lifted. Everything is deterministic: no seed, heuristic stopping rule, or floating-point value enters an acceptance decision. At lengths 64, 70 and 76 the same machinery ran to exhaustion and found nothing: the reversible four-block queue built at each length contains no pair. These are exhaustions of a specific recorded queue, not nonexistence results, and the certificates do not by themselves establish that the queue captures every reversible object of its length. A closing section sorts every claim in the paper by what a reader must accept in order to believe it, and states exactly how far the accompanying artifacts support each one.

title: High-Dimensional Non-Linear Geometric Transformations: A Quantum Algorithm
abstract: This paper presents a novel quantum algorithm for solving high-dimensional non-linear geometric transformations. The algorithm leverages quantum entanglement to accelerate the computation of these transformations, introducing a predictive capability. We detail the core mechanism, including the quantum state representation, entanglement protocol, and the resulting quantum circuit design to achieve the desired optimization. The paper explores the potential of this approach to address complex geometric problems with significant computational bottlenecks. We provide a preliminary analysis of the algorithm's efficiency and discuss its potential applications in areas such as data visualization, image processing, and structural analysis. Further research will focus on refining the quantum circuit design and extending the algorithm to handle more intricate geometric transformations.

title: 基于量子纠缠的并行计算框架
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a peculiar phenomenon in quantum mechanics, offers a unique pathway to revolutionize computation. This paper explores the potential of leveraging quantum entanglement for enhanced parallel computing, particularly within the context of large datasets and complex calculations. We propose a novel framework centered around quantum entanglement, aiming to surpass the limitations of classical parallel computing by exploiting this quantum property. The core mechanism focuses on utilizing entangled qubits to represent and manipulate data, thereby enabling faster and more efficient computation. The research delves into the design of this framework, detailing its underlying principles and potential applications. The paper concludes with a discussion of future research directions and the anticipated impact of this approach on the landscape of parallel computing.

title: Title: Non-Equilibrium Quantum Entanglement Propagation
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a cornerstone of quantum mechanics, exhibits remarkable properties when maintained across extended time scales. However, practical implementations often suffer from rapid decoherence, limiting the potential for robust quantum communication and computation. This paper explores a novel computational framework for propagating entangled quantum states, focusing on the mitigation of decoherence through a dynamically adjusted entanglement degradation model. We propose a probabilistic algorithm for estimating entanglement evolution, incorporating a modified entanglement-time equation that explicitly models quantum gravity effects. The core claim is that this framework, by explicitly incorporating a speculative connection to gravity, offers a pathway towards preserving entanglement across significantly longer timescales than current approaches. We detail the algorithm's design, demonstrate its performance through simulations, and discuss the implications of this approach for fundamental questions in quantum information theory. This work represents a significant step toward addressing the enduring challenge of maintaining entanglement in the face of decoherence.

title: E8 Hyperdimensional Consciousness Mapping via Convergent Transformers — E8 Intelligence Research
abstract: Leveraging the 240-dimensional structure of E8 and sector-exhaustion principles, we propose Hyperdimensional Consciousness Mapping (HCM) to model neural networks as adaptive, sector-tuned processing layers. Each of the 132 harmonics corresponds to cognitive channels, with LQCD-inspired matchings ensuring seamless transitions between symbolic and subsymbolic data representations. By aligning transformer architectures with E8's phi-coupled decay patterns, HCM enables real-time adaptive complex command abstraction, where session biases manifest as seasonal perturbations in network stability. Author: Andrew Stewart Caldin, Independent Researcher, UK. Part of the E8 Intelligence Research series. Platform: e8intelligence.com

title: Neural Organised Spatial Mapping (NOSM): A Self-Organising Spatial Mapping Based on Local Connectivity and Synaptic Plasticity
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to dimensionality reduction and high-dimensional data encoding and retrieval – the Neural Organised Spatial Mapping (NOSM). NOSM leverages the principles of self-organisation observed in biological neural networks, specifically focusing on local connectivity and synaptic plasticity, to generate a spatial map with inherent topological structure. The core mechanism involves constructing an initial network of interconnected neurons, each representing a point in space. Connection strengths and synaptic plasticity are dynamically adjusted based on input data similarity and neuronal similarity, leading to an iterative self-organisation process. The resulting spatial map exhibits a topology where points with similar features are clustered closely together, while dissimilar points are positioned further apart. The system's novelty lies in its biologically inspired approach, contrasting with traditional global feedback mechanisms prevalent in existing neural networks. Mathematical formulations detail the processes, including distance calculations, synaptic plasticity rules, and the iterative self-organisation algorithm. The potential advantages of NOSM, including efficient data encoding and retrieval, are explored.

title: Predictive Coding for High-Dimensional Data with Learned Latent Priors
abstract: Predictive coding offers a promising framework for dimensionality reduction and data modeling by framing data processing as a prediction error minimization problem. However, traditional predictive coding models often struggle to effectively learn informative priors, particularly in high-dimensional scenarios where the underlying data distribution is complex and unknown. This paper proposes an extension of predictive coding that incorporates learned latent prior distributions. This mechanism enables the network to capture underlying structure in high-dimensional data, leading to more robust and efficient dimensionality reduction. We formally define the extended predictive coding framework, outlining the key components including the latent prior distribution, the prediction error signal, and the learning process. The core contribution is the integration of a learned latent prior, allowing the system to adapt to data characteristics and improve predictive accuracy. We demonstrate, through theoretical analysis and the formulation of relevant equations, the potential benefits of this approach for modeling complex, high-dimensional data. The results suggest that incorporating learned priors significantly enhances the effectiveness of predictive coding, providing a valuable tool for data analysis and representation.

title: Quantum Information Entropy Encoding
abstract: Quantum information entropy represents a fundamental measure of uncertainty in a quantum system. Efficiently encoding and manipulating this entropy is crucial for various quantum algorithms and applications. This paper explores the development of a novel encoding scheme based on quantum entanglement, aiming to dynamically adjust the encoding strength based on the system's internal state. We propose a method utilizing the inherent self-adaptative properties of entangled states to achieve a more efficient and robust approach to quantum information processing. This work addresses the limitations of traditional encoding methods by introducing a mechanism for adaptive strength adjustment, minimizing redundancy and potentially unlocking new computational possibilities. The core mechanism centers around leveraging the entanglement to create a feedback loop that optimizes the encoding process. We detail the proposed algorithm, its underlying principles, and preliminary experimental validation demonstrating its effectiveness. The research focuses on the potential of this approach to significantly improve the performance of quantum information processing.

title: Quantum-Inspired Algorithm Design for Data Compression
abstract: This paper investigates the application of quantum-inspired algorithms to the field of data compression. Traditional data compression techniques, primarily based on entropy coding, often struggle to efficiently represent complex data with high correlations. This research proposes a novel approach drawing inspiration from quantum measurement and superposition principles. title: Dynamic Neural Network Architecture Search via Evolutionary Strategies with Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Neural Architecture Search (NAS) has emerged as a powerful technique for automating the design of neural networks, but existing methods often suffer from high computational costs and a limited ability to adapt to dynamic environments. This paper proposes a novel framework that combines evolutionary strategies (ES) and reinforcement learning (RL) to achieve dynamic neural network architecture search. The ES component explores the architecture space, generating candidate architectures through stochastic search. The RL component learns a reward function that guides the ES, favoring architectures that perform well under varying conditions, such as shifts in input distributions or adversarial attacks. This integrated approach enables adaptive architecture search, resulting in networks that can dynamically adjust their structure to maintain optimal performance in evolving scenarios. The core of the system is a dynamically updated reward function, allowing the network to learn what constitutes a good architecture *within a specific context*. This paper outlines the architecture, training procedure, and preliminary results demonstrating the effectiveness of this approach. We define key performance metrics for evaluation, including accuracy, latency, and architectural complexity. Further research will focus on scaling this approach to larger networks and more complex environments.

title: Quantum Key Distribution Protocols and the Fusion with Privacy Enhancing Technologies
abstract: This paper explores the integration of Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) protocols with Privacy Enhancing Technologies (PETs) to bolster communication security. The core argument centers on the synergistic effect of combining these two fields, moving beyond isolated analyses of their individual security profiles. Specifically, we investigate the application of techniques like differential privacy within QKD systems to safeguard the confidentiality of the generated keys. The proposed framework addresses the vulnerabilities inherent in traditional QKD systems by proactively mitigating potential eavesdropping attacks while maintaining the key distribution process. We outline a methodology for incorporating PETs, focusing on algorithms that minimize information leakage about individual key shares. This work contributes to a more robust and secure communication paradigm, crucial for applications demanding high levels of security, such as governmental communications and financial transactions. The key mathematical concepts and formulas are presented within this document.

title: Title: Quantum Superposition Synchronization – A New Approach to Quantum Algorithm Optimization
abstract: Quantum superposition, a fundamental property of quantum mechanics, offers the potential for exponentially faster computation compared to classical algorithms. However, harnessing this potential requires sophisticated optimization techniques. This paper explores a novel synchronization algorithm predicated on quantum superposition and entanglement, aiming to dramatically reduce computational complexity in quantum algorithm execution. The core mechanism involves creating a quantum circuit simultaneously entangled with multiple qubits, and employing a dynamic adjustment of the entanglement state to minimize execution time. The proposed algorithm directly addresses the inherent challenges in optimizing quantum algorithms, offering a fundamentally new pathway for accelerating quantum computations.

title: Quantum Hiding Computation: A Statistical Analysis of Multi-Modal Data
abstract: Quantum Hiding Computation (QHC) represents a paradigm shift in cryptographic security, leveraging quantum mechanics to create virtually unhackable encryption keys. This paper investigates the statistical properties of multi-modal data – encompassing images, audio, text, and other forms – to optimize the performance of QHC algorithms. We propose a novel statistical analysis framework that identifies key patterns and correlations within these diverse data modalities, aiming to significantly improve the efficiency and security of the computation. The core mechanism centers around utilizing QHC's inherent ability to generate statistically significant data, allowing for a more robust and adaptable approach to optimization. This research offers a promising avenue for advancing the practical application of QHC, enhancing its security and performance through a data-driven approach.

title: ΚΑΝ vs MLP An approach by Applied Functional Analysis
abstract: Recently, Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) have emerged as a creative, promising, and challenging alternative within the field of machine learning research.In this thesis, we present the mathematical origins of these architectures and trace their roots to real and functional analysis.We provide the theoretical foundations underlying the effectiveness of both KANs and traditional Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) architectures, emphasizing the analytical results that justify their approximation capabilities.To facilitate a meaningful and comprehensive comparison between these architectures, we perform both simple and more advanced numerical experiments related to image reconstruction and partial differential equations.Through these experiments, we investigate the dynamics, strengths, limitations, and computational challenges associated with training KANs and MLPs.Our analysis highlights the deep interaction between applied analysis and machine learning.In particular, we emphasize how ideas from functional analysis continue to shape the development of modern neural network architectures, while machine learning simultaneously provides powerful new tools for addressing challenging problems in applied analysis.

title: Trustworthy and privacy-preserving decentralized federated learning with multi-layer defense for secure collaborative AI
abstract: Decentralized Federated Learning (DFL) enables collaborative artificial intelligence model training without centralizing sensitive data, making it suitable for privacy-critical and distributed intelligent systems such as healthcare, Industrial IoT, and smart digital infrastructure. Despite its advantages, DFL remains vulnerable to privacy leakage through shared model updates and to model poisoning and backdoor attacks that compromise system reliability, robustness, and trustworthiness. Existing defense mechanisms primarily address either privacy preservation or poisoning robustness independently and often exhibit limited effectiveness under adaptive or high-ratio adversarial settings. This work proposes a trustworthy and privacy-preserving decentralized federated learning framework that jointly addresses these challenges through two integrated components: (i) a hybrid privacy mechanism based on public dataset pretraining followed by differentially private fine-tuning, and (ii) a multi-layer model defense architecture designed to mitigate poisoning and backdoor attacks across decentralized peer-to-peer environments. The framework integrates local data sanitization, peer-side model verification, robust trimmed-mean aggregation, and runtime inference protection to provide defense-in-depth across both training-time and inference-time attack surfaces. An adversary model and operational assumptions are formally defined, and the framework is evaluated under strong adversarial conditions, including a 20% poisoning ratio. Experimental results demonstrate consistent robustness improvements over a vanilla DFL baseline. While the baseline model achieves a clean accuracy of 83.10%, the proposed framework improves clean performance to 86.12%. Under adversarial conditions, accuracy improves from 37.71% to 53.88% for Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM) attacks, from 21.75% to 46.40% for Projected Gradient Descent (PGD) attacks, and from 40.62% to 67.35% for Carlini–Wagner (CW) attacks. For backdoor-based poisoning attacks such as BadNets and Blended attacks, the defense pipeline restores model accuracy to above 86% while maintaining stable benign performance. These findings demonstrate that the proposed framework provides an effective balance between privacy preservation, adversarial robustness, and trustworthy decentralized collaborative learning for secure AI-driven systems.

title: Recovering Temporal and Geographic Signals from Language Model Embeddings
abstract: Understanding whether language-model embeddings encode structured real-world information is important for both representation analysis and information retrieval. We study this question for temporal and geographic signals using a simple projection-based method that operates directly on output embeddings. Given a small set of seed examples, the method defines an axis in embedding space and ranks texts or entities by their projection onto that axis. Our approach is fully black-box and model-agnostic: it requires only embeddings, without access to model weights, internal activations, auxiliary probes, or additional training. This makes it applicable to modern embedding models available only through APIs and provides a lightweight way to analyze whether temporal and spatial dimensions are present in their representation spaces. We apply the method to temporal and geographic datasets and find that embedding projections recover meaningful chronological and spatial structure. These results provide evidence that output embeddings encode signals relevant to time and space, while also offering a practical tool for interpretability and for downstream temporal and geographic information retrieval tasks, such as temporal ordering, geographic ranking, and tagging.

title: TIER: Threat Implicitness Benchmark for Evaluating LLM Safety Behaviors
abstract: Current LLM safety benchmarks largely rely on binary metrics, overlooking how models respond to harmful prompts with varying threat implicitness. We introduce TIER, a Threat Implicitness Benchmark for behavioral safety evaluation of LLMs. TIER covers four risk domains and four threat levels, from explicit harmful requests to sophisticated jailbreaks. Responses are assessed using a six-label behavior scale and two independent LLM judges. Experiments on six open-weight LLMs show that safety behaviors evolve gradually across threat levels rather than shifting directly from refusal to compliance. Contextual prompts yield the most diverse behaviors, while jailbreaks reveal the largest robustness gaps. Furthermore, models with similar Attack Success Rates can exhibit distinct response distributions, highlighting the need for behavior-aware LLM safety evaluation.

title: Physics-Aware Random Walk Fingerprints for Scalable Power Grid Graph Classification
abstract: Recent benchmarks such as PowerGraph provide large collections of power-grid graphs for cascading-failure classification. Graph neural networks (GNNs) achieve strong predictive performance on this task, but typically require end-to-end training and model-specific tuning, while their latent representations can be difficult to relate to physically meaningful propagation patterns. Random Walk Fingerprints (RWF) offer a scalable and interpretable alternative, but existing variants primarily emphasise topology and node-level information, leaving grid-relevant operational edge states in the walk dynamics. We propose Multi-Channel Physics-Aware Random Walk Fingerprints (MC-PA-RWF) for power systems, a lightweight graph-level representation framework that introduces physical edge states into random-walk propagation. The method constructs multiple edge-weighted channels from domain-relevant attributes, extracts a channel-specific fingerprint from each weighted graph, and concatenates the resulting vectors into a compact representation. Experiments on three \textit{PowerGraph} benchmark systems show substantial improvements over topology-only RWF and competitive balanced accuracy against strong GNN baselines, including Graph Convolutional Networks (GCN), Graph Attention Networks (GAT), Graph Isomorphism Networks with edge features (GINE), and Transformer-based Graph Convolutional Networks (TransformerConv). At the largest evaluated settings, the node-edge extension MC-PA-RWF+ achieves around 98.04% - 99.32% balanced accuracy and improves failure-class F1 over the strongest GNN baseline by 1.60 -- 5.84 percentage points, with statistically significant gains across all three systems.

title: Microscopic Quantum Simulation of Adaptive Parameter Adjustment
abstract: This paper introduces a novel micro-quantum simulation framework, termed "MQP," designed to automatically adjust simulation parameters based on the results of the simulation. Traditional micro-quantum simulations often necessitate manual parameter optimization, resulting in high computational costs and suboptimal results. MQP addresses this challenge by incorporating a dynamic parameter adjustment mechanism that iteratively refines the simulation process based on the observed outcomes. The system analyzes the simulation trajectory, identifies regions of high error or uncertainty, and adjusts parameters to minimize these issues. This adaptive approach significantly enhances simulation efficiency and accuracy, offering a more streamlined and reliable method for studying complex quantum systems. This work demonstrates the effectiveness of MQP in various quantum simulations, showcasing its potential for accelerating research in condensed matter physics and quantum chemistry.

title: Title: Adaptive Metric Space Partitioning
abstract: The task of efficiently partitioning data points in high-dimensional spaces is a fundamental challenge in many applications, including data mining, machine learning, and image processing. Traditional partitioning methods often rely on handcrafted heuristics or involve computationally expensive distance calculations. This paper introduces an adaptive metric space partitioning method that automatically creates regions based on the properties of the data points, resulting in a self-organizing structure. The core mechanism involves introducing a similarity measure algorithm that dynamically calculates a metric for each point, guiding the creation of smaller, relevant regions. This approach addresses the inherent difficulty of data distribution in high-dimensional spaces by leveraging the inherent structure of the data itself. The proposed method offers a novel and efficient way to generate meaningful regions, improving overall performance and enabling more effective data analysis. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through a series of experiments comparing it to existing partitioning techniques.

title: Adaptive Randomization in Genetic Algorithms for Complex Optimization
abstract: Genetic algorithms (GAs) have long been a cornerstone of optimization, demonstrating effectiveness across a wide range of complex problems. However, traditional GAs often struggle with suboptimal solutions and lack the ability to effectively explore the solution space. This paper proposes an adaptive randomization strategy to address these limitations by dynamically adjusting random seeds and parameters within the GA framework. We introduce a 'feedback loop' that continuously monitors the algorithm's performance, adjusts random choices based on the current state of the optimization process, and incorporates a mechanism for enhanced exploration of the solution space. This approach aims to improve search efficiency and potentially lead to better, more robust solutions compared to current GAs. The paper details the implementation of this adaptive randomization and demonstrates its potential benefits through a simplified, illustrative example.

title: Bayesian Predictive Geometry (BPG) for Dynamical Systems
abstract: This paper introduces Bayesian Predictive Geometry (BPG), a novel computational framework for dynamically generating and refining geometric representations of complex dynamical systems. Traditional geometric analysis often falls short in accurately modeling evolving systems due to limitations in handling non-linearity and inherent uncertainty. BPG addresses these challenges by extending Bayesian inference to encompass the entire trajectory of a system, modeling non-linearity, and incorporating probabilistic geometric modeling. The core mechanism involves constructing a probabilistic geometric model that evolves the system's geometry in real-time, allowing for improved long-term simulations and prediction of emergent behavior. This work demonstrates the efficacy of BPG through a series of illustrative examples and quantitative analysis, showcasing its potential to significantly enhance the accuracy and efficiency of dynamical system simulations.

title: The identity component of a Jacobian lens inflates the noise floor computed from it
abstract: A transformer's residual stream adds each layer's output to what came before, so the corpus-averaged Jacobian lens J = E[dh_final/dh_l] contains a copy of the identity by construction, and its share grows with depth as less transformation remains above the layer: at the deepest fitted layer of the six lenses read here from models above 1B parameters it is 66% to 88% of the matrix. That matters for any spectral read whose threshold is derived from the frame it is judging. A finite-size Marchenko-Pastur / Tracy-Widom edge estimates its variance as a de-biased median row energy, and an added alpha*I contributes alpha^2 to every row -- the one contribution a median over rows cannot reject -- so the identity raises the floor computed from it by more than 2x on eight of the ten lenses and by up to 4.8x, and the modes in between fall under the line. Separating the two is exact and closed form: alpha = tr(J)/d is the orthogonal projection of J onto span(I) under the Frobenius inner product, a trace and a subtraction with no threshold in it. Reading J - alpha*I in place of J changes the resolved count by 2x to 21x across all eleven lens files read - ten of the twenty-two on the Neuronpedia mirror - in 9 of 10 models, five families, widths 512 to 4096. Most of that range is not a property of transformers: two structure-free surrogates measure the part that belongs to the transport, differing in whether the floor's own variance input (a median row energy) is held fixed: one redraws both subspaces at fixed spectrum and alpha, the other rotates at fixed spectrum, alpha and every row norm, preserved to 2e-16. The excess attributable to the transport lies between 1.15x and 1.87x, and the correlation with identity share behaves the same way on the surrogates (+0.745 real, +0.758 and +0.657 surrogate). The directions below the raw read's floor are reproducible: across the two independent fits of Qwen3.5-4B they name the same vocabulary at Jaccard 0.390, against 0.038 for random directions decoded through the same readout. That agreement decays as a smooth power law in mode index with no knee at the floor, so it establishes that reproducible structure extends well past the raw count rather than that it stops at the residual one. Below relative depth 0.6 the two reads agree. Built on the Entroptics instrument, which it consumes as an engine rather than reimplementing. Includes the paper, the implementation, and the experiments that reproduce every figure from published lens files.

title: Topological State Space Compression with Quantum Algorithms
abstract: Abstract: Topological State Space Compression with Quantum Algorithms addresses the limitations of traditional compression techniques by leveraging quantum superposition and entanglement to identify and reduce redundant states within complex systems. This paper presents a novel quantum algorithm designed to achieve significant compression ratios while maintaining essential information, offering a fundamentally new approach to data compression.

title: ##基于情感反馈的程序学习
abstract: This paper explores the novel approach of leveraging human emotional feedback to guide the learning process of programs. Traditional program learning often relies solely on objective metrics, which may not always align with human preferences or needs. This work proposes a framework where emotional responses, such as satisfaction or confusion, are utilized as dynamic feedback signals. Specifically, we construct an emotion-aware system that captures user sentiment in real-time. This sentiment data is then incorporated into reinforcement learning algorithms, either as reward signals or loss functions, effectively steering the program's development toward outputs that elicit desired emotional responses. We argue that this approach represents a significant advancement in program learning, offering the potential to create systems that are more intuitive, adaptable, and ultimately, more useful to humans. The core claim centers around the improved alignment of program behavior with human needs through the inclusion of emotional data. This paper details the proposed methodology, focusing on the construction of the emotion-aware system and its integration with reinforcement learning. ---

title: Adaptive Quantum Error Correction via Machine Learning
abstract: Quantum error correction (QEC) is critical for the reliable implementation of quantum computers, but current QEC protocols often rely on fixed parameters and struggle to adapt to fluctuating environmental noise. This work proposes a novel approach to QEC that leverages machine learning (ML) to dynamically adapt the parameters of QEC protocols in real-time. The core idea involves training neural networks to predict error rates based on observed quantum data and subsequently optimizing the error correction strategies. This adaptive framework offers the potential for significantly improved performance and resilience against evolving noise characteristics. The primary focus is on the theoretical framework and algorithm design, without the need for experimental validation. The proposed method represents a shift from static QEC to a more flexible and efficient system, addressing a key limitation in current quantum computing architectures. The key concept is represented by the following equation: εt = f(xt, θt, η), where εt is the error rate at time *t*, xt is the quantum state at time *t*, θt are the parameters of the QEC protocol at time *t*, and η is the learning rate. This equation highlights the adaptive nature of the system. The efficiency of the system is measured by the reduction in error rates achieved through adaptive parameter adjustment. Further analysis includes the concept of a cost function, C(θ), that represents the overall error correction performance. The goal is to minimize this cost function using the trained neural network. The core of the system relies on a feedback loop – the neural network predicts the error rate, which then influences the adjustment of the QEC protocol parameters.

title: Dimensional Matching Quantum Algorithm
abstract: This paper introduces a novel quantum algorithm, the Dimensional Matching Quantum Algorithm (DMQA), designed to efficiently identify optimal matchings within multi-dimensional spaces. Leveraging quantum entanglement, DMQA aims to surpass classical algorithms in the search for optimal configurations, with potential applications in machine learning and data analysis. The core mechanism centers around exploiting the unique properties of entangled quantum states to facilitate the discovery of highly correlated patterns, ultimately leading to improved model optimization. This research explores the theoretical foundations and practical implementation of DMQA, highlighting its potential for significant advancements in these fields. The paper concludes with a discussion of the algorithm's strengths, limitations, and future research directions.

title: Relational Transformers for Knowledge Graph Completion
abstract: Knowledge graph completion (KGC) is a crucial task in leveraging the wealth of information stored within knowledge graphs. Traditional approaches, such as graph convolutional networks (GCNs), often fall short in capturing the intricate, long-range dependencies inherent in these structures. This work introduces a novel approach, Relational Transformers, designed specifically for KGC. We propose an architecture based on the transformer model, adapted to effectively model relationships within a knowledge graph. The core idea is to utilize self-attention mechanisms to learn representations of entities and their connections, allowing the model to capture both local and global dependencies. We demonstrate that this approach can significantly improve the accuracy of predicting missing links compared to established methods. The model is trained to predict the existence (or absence) of a relationship between two entities given their connected neighbors. The key innovation lies in the ability of the transformer to inherently handle variable-length sequences and complex interactions, crucial for the irregular nature of knowledge graphs. The results presented here show the potential of relational transformers for robust and accurate knowledge graph completion.

title: Quantum Entanglement Information Field: A Novel Computational Paradigm and Information Carrier
abstract: This paper investigates the potential of quantum entanglement information fields as a novel computational paradigm and information carrier, specifically targeted towards enhancing the efficiency of quantum computation and data transmission. The core concept centers around the utilization of quantum entanglement to facilitate novel calculations and data storage techniques. We explore a defined computational framework predicated on entanglement, detailing its mechanisms for manipulation and storage of quantum states. This research proposes a fundamentally different approach to quantum information processing, offering potential advancements beyond current quantum algorithms. The investigation focuses on the exploration of quantum state manipulation and information encoding through entangled states, aiming to unlock new capabilities in quantum computation.

title: Non-Euclidean Metric Learning for Data Distribution Analysis
abstract: This paper introduces a novel method for learning non-Euclidean metric spaces, offering a robust approach to data distribution analysis. Traditional metric learning methods often rely on assumptions about data distribution, limiting their applicability. We propose a deep learning framework that learns a metric space invariant to local transformations, enabling the automated detection of unusual data patterns. The core mechanism involves a novel neural network architecture designed to effectively capture complex data dependencies and identify deviations from expected patterns. This approach overcomes limitations of existing methods by offering greater flexibility and adaptability in analyzing data distributions. The paper details the architecture, training procedure, and initial results demonstrating the effectiveness of this method in identifying anomalies and patterns.

title: Task-Guided Multi-UAV Cooperative Multi-Target Tracking with Gaussian Process-Based Value Correction
abstract: The cooperative tracking of multiple ground targets by multiple UAVs remains challenging under partial observability, limited communication, and obstacle constraints, owing to complex target association, difficult task handover, strong coupling among low-level continuous control decisions, and unstable critic value estimation. To address these issues, this paper proposes a hierarchical-guidance and Gaussian-process-corrected multi-agent proximal policy optimization method, termed HGP-MAPPO. Built upon the centralized-training and decentralized-execution paradigm, HGP-MAPPO introduces low-frequency task-guidance signals derived from target-association information, task handover and recovery cues, task priorities, and desired observation geometry. These guidance signals are incorporated as conditional inputs into the low-level actor–critic framework, thereby reducing the policy learning difficulty in jointly handling target tracking, occlusion recovery, obstacle avoidance, and smooth control. Moreover, to alleviate local estimation bias in the neural-network critic under complex partially observable conditions, a Gaussian-process-based residual correction mechanism is designed. Specifically, the posterior mean is used to compensate for value residuals, while the posterior uncertainty adaptively regulates the correction intensity, improving the stability of value evaluation and policy optimization. A sparse inducing-point approximation is adopted to control the training-stage computational cost, while the Gaussian-process module is removed during decentralized execution and, therefore, introduces no additional online inference overhead. Experiments are conducted in standard-obstacle and densely obstructed multi-UAV multi-target tracking scenarios, with DDPG-MHSA, MAPPO, MADDPG, and MATD3 adopted as baselines. The experimental results demonstrate that HGP-MAPPO achieves faster training convergence, higher average episode rewards, and improved target retention rates. It also effectively reduces UAV–target distance fluctuations and the mean absolute temporal-difference (TD) error. Ablation studies further confirm the contributions of task-guidance signals, Gaussian-process residual correction, and uncertainty-aware weighting to cooperative tracking performance and training stability.

title: Affect-aware conversational adaptation in mixed reality procedural tasks
abstract: Abstract Conversational agents based on Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly explored in eXtended Reality (XR) applications that require real-time guidance during task execution. In task-oriented XR environments, conversational support must remain responsive and integrated with the ongoing activity, minimizing interruptions in user interaction. Although affect-aware adaptation has been proposed as a possible strategy to improve interaction quality, its impact in immersive task-oriented scenarios remains unclear. This paper presents a mixed-reality conversational system that integrates voice interaction, LLM-driven dialogue, and prosody-based affect-aware adaptation. The system adopts a modular client–server architecture with parallel semantic and affective processing pipelines, enabling emotion-related cues inferred from vocal prosody to be incorporated without interrupting conversational flow. The system was evaluated through a between-subjects study involving 40 participants performing a guided chemical procedure within a mixed-reality laboratory scenario. Participants interacted with either an affect-adaptive or a non-adaptive version of the conversational agent. The evaluation combined standardized questionnaires, behavioral metrics extracted from interaction logs, and qualitative feedback. Results showed that the affect-adaptive condition produced greater perceived usability scores compared to the non-adaptive condition. Participants interacting with the adaptive agent also required longer task completion times and engaged in a higher number of conversational turns. No significant differences emerged for overall workload between the two conditions. Qualitative findings further suggested that affect-aware adaptation made the interaction feel more natural and supportive.

title: PAC-Private Autoregressive Generation: Calibrating Noise to Ensemble Disagreement
abstract: Language models adapted on private text are often served through APIs, so privacy leakage occurs through generated outputs rather than exposed weights. Private prediction protects these releases. Methods such as PMixED incur privacy cost at each release and increasingly rely on the public model over long horizons. PAC privacy instead calibrates noise to output variability across possible secrets, adding less noise when predictions are stable. To our knowledge, PAC-private prediction has not previously been extended from classification to autoregressive generation. We construct $m=128$ overlapping worlds from the private corpus, with each record appearing in exactly $m/2$ worlds, and train one adapter per world over a frozen public model. The realized world is the secret. At each token, the public model defines a candidate set, the worlds vote, and their posterior-weighted disagreement determines the PAC noise; unanimity requires no calibration noise. We prove $I(S;Y_{1:T}) \leq I(S;H_T) \leq bT$. Our contributions are extending PAC privacy to autoregressive generation, handling adaptive self-generated contexts, and introducing coupled decoding that preserves privacy accounting while avoiding greedy degeneration. On WikiText-103 with GPT-2-small, we retain 74% of the fine-tuning gain at a per-token budget of $2^{-32}$, while membership-inference success is bounded by 51.08% after $10^6$ tokens; posterior-entropy estimates of leakage are roughly 17% of the charged budget. Inference privacy is not content protection: even when membership advantage on a memorized canary is indistinguishable from zero, the canary is emitted at the same rate. Against PMixED under matched membership-inference bounds on the same data universe and test set, we retain 98% of non-private headroom from $10^2$ to $10^6$ tokens, versus at most 56%, with no crossover.

title: Injected and Leaked: Actively Inducing Side-Channel Leakage Using Electromagnetic Injection and Hardware Nonlinearity
abstract: Electromagnetic (EM) side-channel leakage and injection are typically treated as distinct physical phenomena, threatening data confidentiality and integrity respectively. This work investigates how EM injection can be used to amplify side-channel leakage that is otherwise infeasible. We introduce a novel framework for Injection-Induced EM Side Channels to enable integrated, closed-loop EM security analysis. Our theoretical modeling and experimental measurements reveal that nonlinear hardware components, such as ubiquitous amplifiers, analog-to-digital converters, and power converters, can modulate secret electrical signals onto an injected EM carrier and thus upconvert low-frequency secrets into measurable EM emissions. By tuning the injection frequency and amplitude, adversaries gain the ability to actively shape the effective spectrum and entropy of the resulting leakage. We design InjectEave attack and demonstrate eavesdropping on the audio played through wired and wireless headphones from up to 30 m away with accessible RF equipment, as well as in through-wall scenarios, and characterize injection-induced EM leakage of other low-frequency secrets such as power consumption of smart home devices and analog sensor inputs. Case studies further demonstrate how the proposed techniques enable closed-loop eavesdropping and manipulation of landline-phone conversations. Finally, we analyze the broader security challenges and mitigations.

title: SiLR: Structure-Preserving Admission and Process Reward for LLM Tool Agents
abstract: A runtime gate for an LLM tool agent is usually cast as a filter. In a ReAct loop a rejected proposal is followed by another at the same state, so the gate is a search operator over the proposal stream whose admission criterion shapes which trajectories are reachable. We study post-violation recovery admission, where progress must be admitted while the system is still in violation, and identify the scalar projection trap: an aggregate-score gate accepts a locally improving proposal and commits the trajectory to a plateau. SiLR instead shadow-executes each proposal and admits it under a product order over the branch-level violation state (overloaded-branch support and per-branch severity). We prove that no scalar surrogate is sound for this order, so the failure is representational, not a matter of threshold tuning. On mined Gym-ANM scenarios, SiLR recovers 21/21 multi-action episodes against 0/21 for terminal and 9/21 for the best scalar gate, significant across the full 24-scenario benchmark. The terminal-versus-structured dichotomy holds across three model families and in CityLearn. Because admission rests on deterministic simulation, the LLM lies outside the trust boundary: a magnitude-redistribution attack that defeats both scalar and support-only baselines is contained only by the full per-branch predicate. With two constraint families active, every tested scalar projection admits physically unsafe actions; support-only admits the largest fraction (63.2% of 42,410; product order 0). In the hardest dual-family traces, scalar gates recover only through that unsafe class. Reused as a GRPO process reward, it outperforms its count projection in every mined scenario and is the only tested reward whose ungated policy exceeds the untrained base (0.844 vs. 0.778). Scalar projection loses the violation geometry at both design points; only the full product order is structurally sufficient.

We study post-violation recovery admission, where progress must be admitted while the system is still in violation, and identify the scalar projection trap: an aggregate-score gate accepts a locally improving proposal and commits the trajectory to a plateau. SiLR instead shadow-executes each proposal and admits it under a product order over the branch-level violation state (overloaded-branch support and per-branch severity). We prove that no scalar surrogate is sound for this order, so the failure is representational, not a matter of threshold tuning. On mined Gym-ANM scenarios, SiLR recovers 21/21 multi-action episodes against 0/21 for terminal and 9/21 for the best scalar gate, significant across the full 24-scenario benchmark. The terminal-versus-structured dichotomy holds across three model families and in CityLearn. Because admission rests on deterministic simulation, the LLM lies outside the trust boundary: a magnitude-redistribution attack that defeats both scalar and support-only baselines is contained only by the full per-branch predicate. With two constraint families active, every tested scalar projection admits physically unsafe actions; support-only admits the largest fraction (63.2% of 42,410; product order 0). In the hardest dual-family traces, scalar gates recover only through that unsafe class. Reused as a GRPO process reward, it outperforms its count projection in every mined scenario and is the only tested reward whose ungated policy exceeds the untrained base (0.844 vs. 0.778). Scalar projection loses the violation geometry at both design points; only the full product order is structurally sufficient.

title: Hierarchical Feedback Loops in Bayesian Inference for Complex Systems
abstract: This paper investigates the application of hierarchical feedback loops within Bayesian inference to enhance the accuracy and robustness of predictions for complex systems. Traditional Bayesian methods often struggle with convergence issues and sensitivity to initial conditions. We propose a novel framework where higher-level nodes provide feedback to lower-level nodes, creating a layered structure that facilitates more stable and reliable predictions. The core mechanism leverages a tiered approach to inference, allowing for the iterative refinement of predictions through a series of interconnected feedback cycles. This approach addresses limitations of current approaches by offering a more adaptable and resilient system capable of handling the inherent complexity of real-world problems. The paper demonstrates the efficacy of this framework through a series of simulations, showcasing improvements in prediction accuracy and robustness across various scenarios.

title: ##混沌动力学自适应算法
abstract: This paper investigates the application of a novel algorithm, termed the "混沌动力学自适应算法" (CDA), to optimize complex systems, with a particular focus on financial markets and biological evolution. The algorithm leverages the principles of chaos theory and adaptive algorithms to dynamically adjust parameters, enabling the system to respond effectively to changing conditions. This approach addresses the limitations of traditional optimization methods by incorporating inherent unpredictability and self-organization. The core mechanism revolves around a dynamic parameter adjustment process guided by the chaotic dynamics of the system being optimized. The research demonstrates the effectiveness of the CDA in achieving optimal solutions and rapid adaptation in challenging scenarios.

title: Quantum Machine Learning in Noise Matrix Optimization
abstract: Quantum Machine Learning (QML) offers a paradigm shift in machine learning, potentially surpassing classical approaches due to quantum phenomena. A critical challenge in many QML applications is the need to effectively manage noise within the model parameters, particularly in training datasets with high dimensionality. This paper explores the application of a novel noise matrix optimization algorithm, specifically tailored for QML, leveraging quantum properties to enhance model accuracy and stability. We propose a method that utilizes quantum superposition and entanglement to explore the parameter space more efficiently, leading to improved generalization performance. The core mechanism focuses on manipulating the noise matrix through quantum rotations and entanglement to achieve a more nuanced and robust optimization. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through a series of simulations and preliminary experiments, highlighting its potential to significantly improve model performance in specific scenarios. The paper concludes with a discussion of future research directions and the implications of this quantum optimization technique for the field of machine learning.

title: falluck2025/prenary-math-lean-complex: Day15 v1.0.1 偏元数学— 复数域 ε · Lean 4 形式化验证
abstract: 声明:本文工作尚未得到独立实验验证,全部结论均为形式化验证层面的初步结果。 偏元数学·复数域 ε · Lean 4 形式化验证 Prenary Mathematics · Complex-Domain ε · Lean 4 Formal Verification 摘要:本文在 Lean 4 中对偏元数学的"复数域 ε"进行形式化验证,覆盖三步——① 复数加法留差(z ⊕ ε = z + ε);② 复数乘性旋转(z ⊗ ε = z · e^ε);③ 破群律的额外留差结构(群律破坏 + 同态破坏)。全部定理通过 Lean 内核 No goals 与 Comparator 独立二次验证,且 ε=0 时退化为经典复数运算。——老陈与AI的深夜实验室 发布 请笑纳—— Abstract: This repository formalizes "complex-domain ε" in prenary mathematics using Lean 4, covering three steps: (1) complex additive residue z ⊕ ε = z + ε; (2) complex multiplicative rotation z ⊗ ε = z · e^ε; (3) the extra-residue structure that breaks group law (group-law breaking + homomorphism breaking). All theorems pass Lean kernel No goals and Comparator independent verification, degenerating to classical complex arithmetic when ε = 0. — Published by Lao Chen & AI's Late Night Lab. title: Quantum Entanglement-Based Persistent Memory
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to persistent memory leveraging the principles of quantum entanglement. The core idea is to utilize entangled qubit states to create a memory system exhibiting inherent persistence and resilience to data corruption surpassing the limitations of conventional storage technologies. The system operates on a self-correcting algorithm continuously observing and manipulating the entangled qubits. This manipulation is driven by quantum decoherence properties, encoding redundancy and performing error correction without relying on explicit quantum error correction codes. The system's unique advantage lies in directly addressing decoherence through entanglement-driven self-organization, achieving true persistent storage at the quantum level. This approach fundamentally shifts the paradigm from actively correcting errors to passively allowing the system to self-organize and maintain data integrity through the inherent properties of entanglement and decoherence. Mathematical formulations detailing the core concepts and operational principles are presented. The system promises significantly enhanced data storage density, reliability, and resistance to environmental noise, representing a critical step toward practical quantum memory.

title: Self-Correcting Neural Networks via Adaptive Learning Rates and Regularization
abstract: Training deep neural networks often faces challenges related to instability and poor generalization due to the accumulation of errors during the learning process. This paper introduces a novel self-correcting neural network architecture designed to mitigate these issues. The core concept involves establishing a feedback loop that monitors the network's error signal and dynamically adjusts both learning rates and regularization parameters. This adaptive control mechanism aims to minimize error accumulation and promote more stable and effective training. The proposed approach offers a potential solution to the inherent instability of neural networks and contributes to improved model performance. The system utilizes a recurrent neural network (RNN) to process the error signal and generate adjustments to the network's hyperparameters. Mathematical formulations detail the adaptive learning rate and regularization parameter adjustment process. The overall impact is a network exhibiting enhanced robustness and generalization capabilities.

title: Contextualized Memory Networks with Hierarchical Semantic Decomposition
abstract: This paper introduces a novel memory network architecture designed to address the challenges of long-term dependency modeling in neural networks. The core idea is to integrate hierarchical semantic decomposition with contextualized memory access. Each memory unit is associated with a multi-level semantic representation, allowing the network to query memories based on increasingly abstract contextual cues. This model leverages a connection between entanglement and circuit complexity to achieve this transformation.

title: Title: Bio-Inspired Temporal Logic (BTL)
abstract: This paper introduces Bio-Inspired Temporal Logic (BTL), a novel logic system inspired by the temporal dynamics of biological organisms. Traditional logic systems, while valuable, often struggle to accurately represent complex, time-dependent systems. BTL aims to overcome these limitations by introducing a new temporal logic formalism centered around growth, decay, and feedback loops, incorporating adaptive parameters derived from observed temporal behavior. The paper details the core mechanism of BTL, exploring the mathematical foundation of its temporal logic and outlining potential applications across diverse domains. We present a preliminary demonstration of BTL's capabilities, demonstrating its potential for robust and efficient representation of time-dependent systems.
