title: QEC-ZURFACE: Sub-Millisecond Classical Decoder Architecture for High-Density Surface Codes under Stochastic Noise
abstract: [ES] Este reporte técnico presenta la evaluación estadística de QEC-ZURFACE (CORE_V16), un motor de enrutamiento clásico optimizado en Python mediante Numba JIT para la mitigación de la decoherencia en códigos de superficie de alta fidelidad. Los resultados experimentales demuestran una capacidad de decodificación nativa sub-milisegundo (916.3 µs) en mallas comerciales masivas de 100x100 (10,000 qubits). Se analizan las métricas de rendimiento frente al framework Google Cirq bajo entornos hostiles de ruido estocástico híbrido, validando la estabilidad y la supresión de falsas alarmas sin requerir clústeres de aceleración masiva. [EN] This technical report presents the statistical evaluation of QEC-ZURFACE (CORE_V16), a classical routing engine optimized in Python via Numba JIT for decoherence mitigation in high-fidelity surface codes. Experimental results demonstrate a native sub-millisecond decoding capacity (916.3 µs) on massive 100x100 commercial meshes (10,000 qubits). Performance metrics are analyzed against the Google Cirq framework under hostile hybrid stochastic noise environments, validating stability and false alarm suppression without requiring massive acceleration clusters. title: Holographic Information Encoding via Entanglement
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to information encoding leveraging the principles of holographic duality and entanglement. We propose a 'coherent entanglement tapestry' – a dynamically modulated layered structure of entangled qubits – capable of storing and retrieving information with unprecedented scalability and adaptability. Traditional quantum computing architectures face limitations in data density and processing speed, necessitating a paradigm shift. This work investigates the potential of this architecture to transcend classical limitations, offering a foundation for future advancements in quantum AI and information processing. We detail the core mechanism, discuss the challenges and benefits of this approach, and present preliminary results demonstrating the potential for significant information encoding and retrieval capabilities.

title: Artifact to supplement the tool-paper: Spectral - Translating Specifications for Deductive Verification into LLVM-IR
abstract: This artifact accompanies the paper “Spectral - Translating Specifications for Deductive Verification into LLVM-IR” which introduces Spectral, a tool that translates specifications from the level of different LLVM based source languages to LLVM-IR. Spectral currently supports specifications for subsets of C, C++ and Swift. This artifact contains the source code of Spectral and the source code of the version of VerCors that has been extended to support Spectral’s specification format. Additionally, the examples that are used in the evaluation of the paper are included. The provided docker image contains executable versions of Spectral and VerCors along with scripts that can be used to replicate the experiments of the paper’s evaluation section (Tables 2 and 3). Additionally, the provided source code of Spectral contains documentation on how to build, use and extend Spectral.

title: Parse2Vec: Transformer Embeddings Deeper than Surface Forms
abstract: Objective: The minimum transformer performance can move forward by incorporating the progress of the last decade. Background: Current efforts begin with surface forms and build meanings for tagging, parsing, identifying semantic relationships, etc. But a parser and outside resources can also provide these morphological, syntactic, and semantic features. Method: Instead of inputting tokens of surface forms into a transformer, we could start with feature vectors whose summed embeddings represent the deep features of the words, changing it to structured data. This is an empirical study on how inputs with feature vectors perform on masked word prediction. Compared to classic transformers, increasing integration between the parser and transformer accumulates to a total accuracy gain of 143% and perplexity loss of 87%.

title: Graph Theory Foundations for Neural Network Models
abstract: This chapter provides a concise introduction to graph-theoretic models of neural networks with an emphasis on their mathematical underpinnings, computational structure, richness of architecture, and utility in applications to real-world problems in various areas. We begin with the foundations of graph theory. With this context, the chapter proceeds to spectral graph theory, the foundation upon which most graph-based machine learning algorithms are built. Graph Laplacian, being a crucial operator in this context, is provided both combinatorically and normalized form, and how their use towards structural relations bound in eigenvalues and eigenvectors. Graph Fourier transform idea is introduced through which filtering as well as convolution becomes feasible within the spectral space. The chapter also redefines traditional neural network architectures in terms of graph theory. A close discussion of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and their extensions forms the basis of the chapter. We also cover classical models such as Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs), which utilize first-order neighborhood propagation to describe spectral convolutions. For social networks, GNNs enable node classification, community detection, and link prediction. Recommender systems use graph-based models of user-item interactions, while GNNs on KG are used to reasoning, relation extraction, and to entities’ disambiguation. Not just application-wise but also as having critically examined existing constraints and continuing research challenges. The chapter ends with the future directions for future graph-based learning development. The future directions are universal graph learning models which can learn to generalize task and domain, combination of graph learning with foundation models and transformers, and construction of neuromyotonic systems combining statistical learning and symbolic reasoning.

title: Trace-Tree Magmas: Proof-Producing Infinite Countermodels and 28 New Order-Five Austin Classifications
abstract: Finite model finders cannot witness an Austin law: an identity whose finite models are all trivial but which has a nontrivial infinite model. We introduce rank-decreasing sparse trace-tree magmas, finitely presented total operations on a countably infinite constructor-tree carrier. The default product pairs its arguments; finitely many positive Horn clauses define exceptions. Our main procedure derives clauses from symbolic evaluation traces. For every model found, it proves functionality of the exceptional relation by descent on constructor size, proves the identity by exhaustive symbolic case analysis, and emits a self-contained Lean 4 certificate. A least simultaneous fixed point gives an implementation-independent semantics, so bounded search may miss models but cannot invalidate certified results. On ETP's 96 order-five Austin candidates, we discover and Lean-verify infinite countermodels for 28 identities with no prior public classification in our audit. They form 14 duality classes and establish 28 new Austin classifications. Four ALPS-known cases bring the total to 32 certified candidates. On Canonical-4187, the deduplicated union of Order5-130 and the 4,141-row ALPS pool, a fresh trace run produces 636 certificates, all accepted by Judge v3. At equal resource limits, Vampire 5.0.1, E 3.5.1, and complete Twee 2.6.1 jointly prove implications in 94 canonical classes. Only Twee returns trusted counter-satisfiable outcomes, for 18 classes; independent finite-side certificates force 16 to be infinite. None of these ATPs emits an explicit model or Lean certificate, and none decides the 28 new classifications. To the best of our audit, this is the first automated system to synthesize this trace-tree model family, generate well-founded inversion proofs, and emit self-contained Lean 4 certificates.

title: How Faithful Is Attribution for Sales Forecasting? A Counterfactual Study
abstract: Deep models for sales forecasting, such as WaveNet-style dilated convolutional networks, are accurate but opaque: when a single model predicts sales for one of many series, it offers no account of why. We add a post-hoc, architecture-agnostic counterfactual interpretability layer to a multi-series WaveNet forecaster trained on the full Corporacion Favorita grocery dataset (174,685 series over 1,688 days). The method decomposes each forecast into contributions that sum exactly to the predicted value, avoiding the allocation artifacts we observed with additive SHAP-style attribution. We evaluate faithfulness with a deletion/insertion protocol and find a statistically significant effect on both tests (deletion gap 0.22, p<0.001; insertion gap 0.27, p<0.01; robust across five background-sampling seeds), establishing that the attributions reflect genuine model behavior rather than plausible-looking artifacts. We then characterize, honestly, where attribution is and is not informative: reliance on the promotion signal is heterogeneous across series (median ratio approximately 1.0, with roughly 20% of series showing a strong effect), and the model captures the shape of the weekly sales cycle (day-of-week r=0.78) while systematically under-predicting its amplitude. Our contribution is not improved accuracy but an interpretability layer with a rigorous faithfulness evaluation and a candid account of its limits.

title: When Do Internal Probes Beat Reading the Answer? Miscalibrated Readouts and Behavior-Concealed Knowledge in Language Models
abstract: A 0.6B language model, asked to verify 1,200 logical conclusions (half valid, half corrupted by a single semantic edit), answers YES every time. Judged by behavior it discriminates nothing; linear probes on its hidden states read the correct verdict at 0.96 AUC, transferring to unseen logical structures and separating foils built from exactly the words of the true conclusion (0.90). We ask where the verdict is lost, and find the dominant failure is a single scalar. The verdict survives to the model's own output logits (margin AUC 0.89) along a well-aligned readout direction; a saturated decision threshold, offset by +4.6 sigma, erases it. The diagnosis generalizes: across 90 semantic-label configurations of a five-model, three-family factorial, behavioral accuracy collapses onto a single function of threshold offset (Spearman -0.93) while margin ranking moves far less. Across a 13x scale range, internal knowledge saturates while free-form behavior is non-monotone: an 8B model underperforms its 4B sibling through an answer-channel failure rather than the threshold; forced-choice accuracy is monotone. The diagnosis is actionable: a one-parameter correction, never fit on evaluated structures, repairs behavior from 50% to 81% (0.6B); calibrated margin decoding recovers 94% at 8B; few-shot prompting works the same way, recentering the threshold (+4.6 sigma to 0.0 sigma) while preserving ranking. Comparing probe to margin separates three regimes: concealed, miscalibrated, and undetected. On a maze task built so foils carry no surface cues, the audit correctly reports the third. In the standard generation setting, answer-surface features and heuristic labels reproduce published probing results without any internal access.

evidence.title: When Do Internal Probes Beat Reading the Answer? Miscalibrated Readouts and Behavior-Concealed Knowledge in Language Models
evidence.abstract: A 0.6B language model, asked to verify 1,200 logical conclusions (half valid, half corrupted by a single semantic edit), answers YES every time. Judged by behavior it discriminates nothing; linear probes on its hidden states read the correct verdict at 0.96 AUC, transferring to unseen logical structures and separating foils built from exactly the words of the true conclusion (0.90). We ask where the verdict is lost, and find the dominant failure is a single scalar. The verdict survives to the model's own output logits (margin AUC 0.89) along a well-aligned readout direction; a saturated decision threshold, offset by +4.6 sigma, erases it. The diagnosis generalizes: across 90 semantic-label configurations of a five-model, three-family factorial, behavioral accuracy collapses onto a single function of threshold offset (Spearman -0.93) while margin ranking moves far less. Across a 13x scale range, internal knowledge saturates while free-form behavior is non-monotone: an 8B model underperforms its 4B sibling through an answer-channel failure rather than the threshold; forced-choice accuracy is monotone. The diagnosis is actionable: a one-parameter correction, never fit on evaluated structures, repairs behavior from 50% to 81% (0.6B); calibrated margin decoding recovers 94% at 8B; few-shot prompting works the same way, recentering the threshold (+4.6 sigma to 0.0 sigma) while preserving ranking. Comparing probe to margin separates three regimes: concealed, miscalibrated, and undetected. On a maze task built so foils carry no surface cues, the audit correctly reports the third. In the standard generation setting, answer-surface features and heuristic labels reproduce published probing results without any internal access.

title: Safe Offline Reinforcement Learning: A Survey from Cost Constraints to Feasibility and Learned Safety Certificates
abstract: Safe offline reinforcement learning asks a learner to improve behavior from a fixed dataset while avoiding unsafe decisions at deployment. The problem is more subtle than combining constrained reinforcement learning with offline reinforcement learning: the learner must infer not only what is rewarding, but also what safety means, where safe behavior is supported by data, and how a learned notion of safety should constrain the action that is eventually executed. Recent work has therefore diversified the object used to represent safety. Cost- and value-based methods such as CPQ, COptiDICE, and C2IQL retain the constrained Markov decision process view and make the cost objective increasingly compatible with offline conservatism. A different line, represented by FISOR, SafeFQL, and EpiFlow, treats safety as feasibility or reachability and asks whether a safe continuation exists rather than merely estimating expected cumulative cost. Other approaches infer safety in latent spaces, from weak trajectory-level supervision, through distribution shaping, or from temporal specifications. Most recently, offline-learned control barrier functions, including CCBF and V-OCBF, turn learned safety information into an explicit certificate that can be enforced by a runtime safety filter. This survey is organized by these criteria rather than chronology or individual methods. It develops a common vocabulary for the safety object, the policy-learning mechanism, and the deployment-time enforcement mechanism, and uses this vocabulary to explain relationships among apparently different methods. In particular, the survey examines why FISOR's inference-time rejection mechanism creates a deployment bottleneck, how SafeFQL changes that design while retaining reachability structure, and how V-OCBF connects value-guided offline learning with a CBF-QP safety layer. The survey closes by identifying open problems in finite-data guarantees, support-aware certificate learning, deployment shift, weak safety supervision, and the combination of direct policies with independently enforceable safety certificates.

title: Title: Non-Linear Matrix-Vector Transformations with Dynamic Kernel Selection
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to matrix-vector transformations that incorporates dynamic kernel selection. Traditional methods often rely on a fixed kernel function, which can struggle to adapt to evolving data distributions. This research proposes a meta-learning framework to dynamically learn optimal kernels for each input, enhancing the system's robustness against noise and variations in the data. The core mechanism involves training a meta-learner to optimize the kernel function based on the input data's characteristics, resulting in improved performance and adaptability. We present a comprehensive evaluation of the proposed method on a range of datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness in maintaining accuracy and robustness even with significant data perturbations.

title: Algorithmic Complexity for Evolutionary Algorithms
abstract: Evolutionary algorithms (EAs) are widely employed for optimization problems across diverse fields. However, their computational cost can be a significant bottleneck, particularly when dealing with complex landscapes and large datasets. This paper investigates the algorithmic complexity of EAs, specifically focusing on the design of an evolutionary algorithm tailored to minimize computational expense by introducing a novel hierarchical representation of solutions. We argue that this approach, by breaking down problems and optimizing the solution space itself, offers a potential pathway to more efficient evolution. We detail the core mechanism of hierarchical decomposition and its impact on computational performance, demonstrating empirical results suggesting a substantial reduction in computational cost compared to traditional EAs.

title: Title: Quantum-Enhanced Topological Data Analysis for Signal Processing
abstract: Quantum-enhanced Topological Data Analysis (QETA) presents a novel approach to signal processing, specifically focusing on the extraction of meaningful features from complex data like electroencephalography (EEG) and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI). This paper introduces a quantum-enhanced algorithm designed to overcome the limitations of conventional methods by exploiting quantum interference effects to improve detection accuracy and processing speed. The core mechanism involves utilizing a quantum circuit to perform a computationally intensive feature extraction operation, demonstrating a significant advancement in the field of topological data analysis. We present a preliminary implementation demonstrating the potential of QETA to achieve superior performance in data analysis tasks compared to existing techniques.

title: Self-Adaptive Quantum State Description
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to quantum state description utilizing self-adaptive topology. We propose a method that dynamically links quantum state distribution to topological structure, allowing for precise prediction of quantum state stability and control. Traditional quantum state descriptions often treat topology as an afterthought, hindering a deeper understanding of the underlying quantum properties. This work leverages the inherent properties of topology to provide a more robust and controllable framework for quantum systems. The core mechanism involves a process of mapping quantum states onto a topological space, which then facilitates the prediction of stability and control. The research explores the potential of this approach to enhance quantum information processing and manipulation.

title: Quantum State Space Analysis for Time-Dependent State Detection and Analysis
abstract: Quantum state space analysis offers a novel approach to studying the dynamic behavior of quantum states, particularly focusing on time-dependent evolution. This paper introduces a new algorithm, "Time-Dependent State Space Analysis," designed to efficiently detect and analyze time-dependent patterns within quantum state space. The core mechanism leverages the inherent temporal properties of quantum states to identify crucial dynamics that are often overlooked by traditional methods. We propose a method that systematically tracks the evolution of quantum states over time, identifying statistically significant changes indicative of time-dependent processes. This research aims to improve the efficiency and reliability of quantum computation by providing a robust framework for detecting and mitigating potential errors associated with time-dependent phenomena. The proposed algorithm offers a significant advancement in the field of quantum state analysis, potentially unlocking new possibilities for quantum hardware design and optimization.

title: Geometric Chaos in Algorithmic Search
abstract: This paper investigates the phenomenon of geometric chaos in algorithmic search, exploring a novel strategy inspired by its mathematical properties. We propose a new search algorithm that utilizes stochastic perturbations to mimic random variations in the search path, aiming to overcome the limitations of conventional algorithms in navigating complex search spaces. The core mechanism centers around introducing a controlled randomness into the search process, encouraging exploration of diverse regions of the search space and potentially leading to more globally optimal solutions. The paper presents a theoretical analysis of the algorithm's behavior and provides an initial implementation demonstrating its effectiveness in a simplified search scenario. We quantify the impact of the stochastic perturbation on the search trajectory, demonstrating a significant improvement in coverage and solution quality compared to baseline algorithms.

title: Dimensional Space Protocol
abstract: This paper presents a novel Dimensional Space Protocol (DSP) that leverages quantum entanglement to achieve unprecedented precision in numerical simulations. Traditional methods rely on precise numerical calculations, limiting the potential for accurate results. This protocol introduces a dynamic parameter adjustment mechanism centered around quantum entanglement, allowing the model to intelligently adjust parameters to optimize accuracy and control numerical outcomes. The core mechanism distinguishes this approach by directly integrating quantum entanglement into the core computational process, offering a pathway to significantly enhanced precision and control compared to conventional numerical methods. This research explores the potential of this protocol, detailing its theoretical foundations, implementation considerations, and preliminary results demonstrating significant improvements in accuracy and control.

title: Nonlinear Geometry and Quantum Entanglement: A Coupling Mechanism
abstract: This paper investigates the synergistic potential of nonlinear geometry and quantum entanglement, proposing a novel quantum computing framework based on topological geometry. We explore a new coupling mechanism that leverages geometric transformations to enhance the stability and efficiency of quantum entanglement. The core claim is that by incorporating geometric properties into the entanglement process, we can overcome limitations inherent in traditional quantum entanglement theories and achieve significantly improved quantum key distribution capabilities. This work presents a framework that utilizes a topological structure for quantum entanglement, offering a potential paradigm shift in quantum computation.

title: Adaptive Neuron Activation Functions Based on Multi-Modal Biological Signals
abstract: This paper explores the concept of adaptive neuron activation functions, moving away from the traditional static models used in artificial neural networks. The core argument posits that biological neurons operate with multi-modal input—electrical, chemical, and potentially photonic signals—which dynamically adjust their activation functions. We propose a framework leveraging deep learning to map multi-modal biological signals to adaptive activation functions, mimicking the inherent flexibility and computational efficiency observed in biological systems. The key innovation lies in the dynamic adjustment of neuron activation based on the integrated information from multiple sensory modalities, potentially leading to more robust and nuanced neural network models. This approach addresses limitations of current neural networks by incorporating a more biologically plausible mechanism for computation. The primary goal is to generate activation functions that are not fixed but rather respond intelligently to complex, multi-faceted input, ultimately improving the representational capacity and computational power of artificial neural networks. The theoretical framework and proposed methodology are presented, outlining a pathway for future research in this area.

title: Title: Topological Invariant Optimization Algorithms for Complex Functions
abstract: This paper presents a novel optimization algorithm, dubbed Topological Invariant Optimization (TO), designed to address the inherent challenges in optimization, particularly when dealing with complex functions. Traditional optimization methods often struggle with sensitivity to small changes in the input, leading to suboptimal solutions. TO leverages topological concepts to identify regions of the function space where the function's behavior remains consistent across transformations, guaranteeing results are invariant under these changes. The algorithm employs a novel approach involving the construction of a "topological graph" representing the function's landscape, enabling the identification of these invariant regions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of TO through rigorous analysis and testing, showcasing its ability to outperform existing methods on a variety of complex function optimization problems. The core mechanism is based on the principle of identifying and exploiting topological structures to enhance robustness. The paper concludes with a discussion of the algorithm's theoretical underpinnings and potential applications in diverse fields.

title: Distributed Consensus Algorithms on Quantum Networks
abstract: This paper investigates the development of distributed consensus algorithms specifically designed for quantum networks. The core concept involves utilizing quantum entanglement and superposition to accelerate and strengthen agreement between distributed quantum nodes. The proposed algorithms are built upon quantum communication protocols leveraging Bell inequalities and quantum teleportation. We aim to demonstrate a significant improvement in consensus speed and robustness compared to classical approaches. The theoretical framework presented outlines the key components and mathematical formulations necessary for implementing such protocols. The results suggest that exploiting quantum properties can unlock enhanced distributed computing capabilities, offering potential advantages for secure and efficient distributed systems. The primary focus is on the theoretical design and analysis, without experimental validation.

title: Field-Adaptive Probability Model
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to probabilistic modeling, termed Field-Adaptive Probability Model (FAPM), which leverages domain-specific knowledge to enhance model accuracy within specific application domains. Traditional probabilistic models often suffer from a lack of adaptability, requiring extensive retraining for each new domain. FAPM dynamically integrates domain knowledge into the model's probabilistic framework, resulting in significantly improved predictive performance. This paper details the design of a "Field-Adaptive Probability Update" algorithm, which iteratively refines the model's probability distribution based on the input domain knowledge. We demonstrate the effectiveness of FAPM through a series of comparative analyses across several benchmark datasets, showcasing substantial improvements in accuracy and robustness compared to baseline models. This research emphasizes the crucial role of domain-specific information in creating more effective and adaptable probabilistic models.

title: 基于动态的遗传算法的复杂系统优化
abstract: This paper investigates the application of a dynamic genetic algorithm (DGA) to optimize complex systems. Traditional optimization methods often struggle with the inherent complexity of these systems, requiring significant manual intervention. This research introduces a novel DGA approach that dynamically adjusts genetic algorithm parameters, providing a robust and automated optimization process. The core mechanism focuses on employing a feedback loop to continuously refine the algorithm's parameters based on the system's response to changes. The proposed method demonstrates improved performance compared to traditional approaches in a series of complex system simulations. This work offers a significant advancement in complex system optimization, offering a more flexible and efficient solution.

title: Adaptive Information Entropy
abstract: This paper investigates the application of an adaptive information entropy algorithm to optimize machine learning models. Traditional information entropy methods are often static, failing to fully leverage the dynamic characteristics of training data and model architecture. This work proposes a novel algorithm that dynamically adjusts the complexity of information entropy calculations based on these factors, resulting in enhanced model performance. The core mechanism centers around a feedback loop that adjusts the algorithm's parameters, ensuring optimal parameter selection. We present a detailed analysis of the algorithm's performance compared to baseline methods and explore its potential benefits in various machine learning scenarios.

title: Non-Standard Probability Field Theory: Evolutionary Computation
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to evolutionary computation, utilizing a non-standard probability field theory to simulate and predict the long-term evolution of complex systems. The core mechanism involves iteratively refining a probability field, guided by evolutionary algorithms, to identify optimal "life patterns" that dictate the system's trajectory. The research aims to bridge the gap between traditional probability field models and biological and physical systems, offering a framework for understanding and modeling complex evolution. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach through simulations of a simplified ecological system, illustrating its capability to generate plausible evolutionary pathways and provide insights into system dynamics. This work represents a significant step toward a more adaptive and insightful approach to modeling complex systems.

title: A machine-learning-ready strong-motion dataset for earthquake early warning in Chile (2007-2020)
abstract: Three-component strong-motion waveforms, analyst-reviewed P-wave picks, and peak ground acceleration and velocity labels for 55,651 earthquakes recorded in Chile between November 2007 and July 2020, packaged as a single HDF5 file for machine learning. The dataset contains 407,631 station-event records from 88 accelerometer stations across networks C, C1 and CX, spanning magnitudes M1.0 to M8.2 and hypocentral depths from -4.8 to 337 km. It includes both M8+ earthquakes recorded by the network in this period, the 2014 Iquique and 2015 Illapel mainshocks. Each event stores 30 s of ground acceleration at 100 Hz, aligned to the earliest P-arrival anywhere in the network, together with station coordinates, per-station P-picks, peak ground acceleration and velocity, and the times at which each of five PGA thresholds (1, 2, 5, 10 and 20 %g) was first crossed. PGA labels are measured on the full 180 s record rather than the stored window, so they are not truncated by it. The file uses the same schema as the datasets released with the Transformer Earthquake Alerting Model (TEAM). Hypocentres and picks come from the revised CSN catalogue (Potin et al., 2025); the 2015 Illapel mainshock is absent from that catalogue and was added from the ISC Bulletin. The included README documents the full file structure, conventions and caveats.

title: RAPTOR: Role-Aware Private Training for Mixture-of-Experts
abstract: Differentially private (DP) fine-tuning methods treat sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models as a single dense block, ignoring that shared layers see all data while experts only see routed records. We identify and formally characterize three resulting failure modes: global clipping suppresses expert gradients, batch-level normalization dilutes sparse expert updates, and fixed privacy noise degrades signal-to-noise ratio on low-load experts. We introduce RAPTOR - a Role-Aware Private Training framework, which alternates shared and expert optimization and targets each failure directly, using expert-specific clipping and noise together with a public expected-owner denominator and a count-independent update schedule that avoids conditioning on private, realized expert counts. We prove the resulting mechanism satisfies $(\varepsilon,δ)$-DP: because each record is assigned to exactly one owner expert, per-expert mechanisms within a layer compose in parallel, so updating all $E$ experts costs no more, in privacy terms, than updating one, with shared and expert streams composing sequentially across training. We further derive a bias-variance decomposition of the public-denominator estimator showing its bias grows predictably with routing imbalance, yielding a privacy-free rule for selecting which layer to protect from routing entropy measured on a small public corpus. Experiments on Switch Transformer and OLMoE fine-tuning across GLUE tasks, and on DeepSeek-VL2-Tiny, show consistent gains over standard DP baselines across several privacy levels ($\varepsilon$), with the largest margins typically at the tightest budgets. Code and models are publicly available: https://github.com/leduckhai/RAPTOR

We introduce RAPTOR - a Role-Aware Private Training framework, which alternates shared and expert optimization and targets each failure directly, using expert-specific clipping and noise together with a public expected-owner denominator and a count-independent update schedule that avoids conditioning on private, realized expert counts. We prove the resulting mechanism satisfies $(\varepsilon,δ)$-DP: because each record is assigned to exactly one owner expert, per-expert mechanisms within a layer compose in parallel, so updating all $E$ experts costs no more, in privacy terms, than updating one, with shared and expert streams composing sequentially across training. We further derive a bias-variance decomposition of the public-denominator estimator showing its bias grows predictably with routing imbalance, yielding a privacy-free rule for selecting which layer to protect from routing entropy measured on a small public corpus. Experiments on Switch Transformer and OLMoE fine-tuning across GLUE tasks, and on DeepSeek-VL2-Tiny, show consistent gains over standard DP baselines across several privacy levels ($\varepsilon$), with the largest margins typically at the tightest budgets. Code and models are publicly available: https://github.com/leduckhai/RAPTOR

title: Hadamard Rigidity of Positive Sojourn Time Distributions for Rotation Coins
abstract: We study the distribution of the positive sojourn time for a one-dimensional two state quantum walk, conditioned on return to the origin. Konno showed that, for the Hadamard walk, this conditional distribution is exactly uniform at times divisible by $4$. In this paper, we investigate whether this finite time exact uniformity characterizes the Hadamard coin within the family of rotation coins. For a fixed initial state, we prove that the following three conditions are equivalent for rotation coins: the conditional distribution is exactly uniform at time $8$; the conditional distribution is exactly uniform at every time $4m$ with $m\ge2$; and the coin is the Hadamard coin. Thus, the uniformity phenomenon found by Konno is characterized as a rigidity phenomenon of the Hadamard coin within the rotation coin family. The proof uses a matrix-valued generating function for paths returning to the origin. We analyze the algebraic structure arising from an absorbing process on the half line. Finally, by comparing low degree coefficients at time $8$, we show that exact uniformity forces the rotation coin to be the Hadamard coin.

title: Lindblad Multiproduct Formulas
abstract: We introduce Lindblad Multiproduct Formulas: a quantum error mitigation technique that uses two-dimensional tensor networks contracted with loop-corrected belief propagation. The quantities required to implement the error mitigation scheme that are evaluated with tensor networks can be less computationally expensive to calculate than the expectation values themselves, thus allowing for the possibility of applying our method to certain systems for which tensor network methods may struggle to calculate the observable quantities of interest. The workflow incorporates Clifford rescaling techniques and outputs an estimated error bar. We apply our method to a model of two-dimensional discrete time crystals studied previously and implement it on $65$ qubits arranged in a $3\!\times\!3$ heavy-hexagonal topology on the quantum computer ibm_basquecountry. We show that a GPU implementation of the classical part of our workflow achieves a speedup of up to $5.6\times$.

title: Quantum Machine Learning System State Prediction
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to system state prediction utilizing quantum machine learning (QML) algorithms. Traditional machine learning methods struggle with complex systems due to computational limitations, while QML offers the potential for enhanced accuracy and precision through quantum phenomena. We propose a method that learns the dynamic state changes of a system using quantum machine learning, resulting in significantly improved prediction capabilities. This work introduces a tailored quantum algorithm designed to capture subtle correlations within system states, exceeding the performance of classical methods in several benchmark scenarios. The core mechanism focuses on leveraging quantum entanglement and superposition to represent and manipulate state vectors, enabling more efficient and accurate state prediction. We detail the algorithm's architecture, the quantum circuit implementation, and the resulting performance improvements across a series of carefully selected test cases. The results demonstrate a substantial advancement in system state prediction accuracy, highlighting the potential of QML to revolutionize this critical task.

title: Title: Quantum State Collapse as a Computational Algorithm for Data Compression
abstract: Quantum State Collapse (QSC) presents a novel computational algorithm for data compression based on the principles of quantum mechanics. This paper explores the potential of leveraging quantum entanglement and collapse dynamics to achieve lossless data transfer, offering a fundamentally different approach compared to traditional compression methods. We detail the core mechanism of QSC, outlining the adaptation of Grover's algorithm to specifically address the collapse process and its potential for enhanced information transfer rates. This work investigates the mathematical foundations and computational feasibility of this algorithm, emphasizing its potential to surpass current compression techniques. The paper concludes with a discussion of the challenges and future directions for research in this area.

title: High-Dimensional Probability Graphs: An Optimized Algorithm Through Adaptive Graph Convolutional Networks
abstract: High-dimensional probability graphs represent complex data landscapes, often challenging to analyze and interpret. This paper introduces a novel optimization algorithm, termed Adaptive Graph Convolutional Networks (AGCN), designed to effectively represent and predict data within these high-dimensional spaces. AGCN utilizes a dynamically adjusted graph convolution mechanism, driven by data features and prediction goals, to minimize computational complexity and maximize prediction accuracy. We demonstrate the effectiveness of AGCN through comprehensive experiments on a variety of datasets exhibiting high dimensionality and complex relationships. The core mechanism of AGCN lies in its self-adaptive parameter adjustments, offering a robust and efficient approach to handling high-dimensional data. This work addresses limitations of existing optimization techniques, particularly in the context of complex graph structures and high-dimensional data.

abstract: Quantum entanglement matrix topology analysis and application represents a novel approach to quantum information processing and cryptography, offering enhanced security through the utilization of unique topological properties. This work contributes to the advancement of quantum cryptography by demonstrating the potential for exploiting topological defects within quantum systems.

This inherent flexibility is achieved through the strategic manipulation of the simulation space, leveraging quantum properties to enhance accuracy and resolution. The proposed framework offers a significant advancement in the field, enabling more precise and efficient simulations of complex systems, particularly those requiring nuanced modeling.

title: Cognitive Geometry for Procedural Content Generation
abstract: This paper explores the application of cognitive geometry to procedural content generation. We propose a system that learns and generates levels, landscapes, and other procedural elements by mapping visual representations to underlying cognitive processes. The core mechanism involves training a neural network to translate human cognitive processes – specifically spatial reasoning and pattern recognition – into a geometry-based representation. This approach aims to move beyond rigid rules and towards a more adaptive and intuitive generation process, offering a novel framework for creating dynamic and engaging game worlds and environments. The paper discusses the system's architecture, training methodology, and preliminary results demonstrating the system's ability to produce diverse and consistent procedural content.

title: Title: Phase-Field Quantum Geometry (PFQ)
abstract: The field of quantum geometry is experiencing a resurgence, driven by the desire to understand and manipulate the fundamental structure of quantum systems. This paper introduces the Phase-Field Quantum Geometry (PFQ) framework, a novel approach to representing and manipulating geometric configurations within quantum systems. PFQ leverages the concept of phase fields to dynamically construct complex geometric structures, offering a powerful tool for studying quantum phenomena and potentially enabling new quantum technologies. The core mechanism focuses on an automated "Phase Field Mapping" algorithm, which constructs intricate geometric representations from quantum data. This paper presents a detailed explanation of the PFQ framework, including its mathematical foundations, algorithm implementation, and potential applications across diverse quantum systems. The research explores the advantages of PFQ compared to existing geometric techniques and highlights its potential to unlock deeper insights into quantum mechanics.

title: Telix Design Proposal
abstract: Design proposal for Telix, a research operating-system and toolchain architecture. The document covers the system design - memory, scheduling, filesystem, I/O, clustering, control plane, personality, and polyglot language integration (including a GHC cross-compilation target and a musl libc port) - together with an adversary model and TCB decomposition, isolation primitives, an explicit degradation path, a comparison against seven contemporary systems with the five claims held out as novel, and a three-tier structure for empirical validation (inherited evidence, the page-clustering performance hypothesis, and compositional burden). Claims without prototype evidence are labelled as hypotheses. Dual-licensed: recipients may take this work under EUPL-1.2 or CC BY 4.0, at their option.

abstract: Quantum-Inspired Neural Network Architectures (QINNA) are a novel approach to neural network design that leverages the principles of quantum mechanics, specifically superposition and entanglement, to enhance learning and generalization capabilities. The core mechanism revolves around creating dynamic representations and processing that mimic the inherent properties of quantum systems.

title: Probabilistic Reasoning-Based Program Verification Tool
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to program verification leveraging probabilistic reasoning. Traditional program verification techniques often struggle with programs exhibiting uncertainty or randomness, leading to incomplete or inaccurate results. Our proposed tool addresses this limitation by transforming programs into probabilistic models and employing probabilistic inference algorithms to assess program correctness. The core mechanism involves quantifying program behavior through probability distributions, allowing the verification process to account for inherent uncertainties in execution. This approach expands the scope of program verification, enabling the validation of systems where traditional deterministic methods are inadequate. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated through theoretical analysis and conceptual design, outlining a framework for robust program verification in uncertain environments. The primary goal is to provide a methodology that can handle probabilistic programs and provide a confidence level in the program's correct execution.

title: High-Dimensional Topological Mapping for Dynamic Adaptive Control
abstract: This paper introduces a novel high-dimensional topological mapping technique designed for dynamic adaptive control of complex systems. Traditional topological mapping methods often struggle with high-dimensional data due to computational complexity and limited applicability. We propose a method that dynamically adjusts the topological structure of the system based on the current state, enabling efficient optimization and control. The core mechanism involves applying a dynamic mapping algorithm to the high-dimensional representation of the system, iteratively refining the topology to achieve optimal performance. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach through simulations involving a simulated neural network, showcasing significant improvements in control precision and system stability compared to existing techniques. The key contribution lies in the method's ability to automatically adapt the topology to evolving system dynamics, offering a promising pathway toward more robust and adaptable control systems.

title: Title: Quantum-Inspired Iterative Loop (QIL)
abstract: Quantum-Inspired Iterative Loop (QIL) is a novel algorithmic framework designed to address complex optimization problems by leveraging the principles of quantum mechanics. The core concept revolves around a dynamically evolving iterative loop where mathematical constructs are evaluated against a quantum-inspired probability distribution. This process allows for the exploration of the solution space, ultimately leading to a more refined and effective solution compared to traditional methods. This research explores the potential of QIL to bridge the gap between quantum computing and mathematical reasoning, offering a new approach to tackling challenging optimization scenarios. The system employs a closed-form mathematical model that is continually refined through the application of a quantum-inspired probability distribution, achieving a degree of dynamic adaptation not achievable through conventional iterative techniques. This work presents a theoretical foundation and initial implementation demonstrating the feasibility and potential of QIL for a range of problems, including constrained optimization and combinatorial search.

title: Algorithmic Curiosity-Driven Exploration of Complex Systems
abstract: This paper introduces a novel algorithmic approach to exploration in complex systems, driven by a "curiosity" module. Traditional exploration methods frequently rely on extrinsic rewards or pre-defined metrics, which can significantly limit an agent's capacity to discover genuinely novel insights. This work posits that a more effective strategy involves mimicking the intrinsic motivation observed in animal learning – a drive to explore regions of the state space characterized by high uncertainty or unexpected changes. The proposed algorithm incentivizes agents to actively seek out these "curious" states, leading to more efficient and potentially transformative exploration. We formalize this approach with a mathematical framework, demonstrating its potential to overcome the limitations of conventional exploration strategies. The core concept involves minimizing prediction error and maximizing unexpected state transitions. The key equations are presented below for clarity. The exploration process is then evaluated hypothetically, illustrating the potential advantages of this curiosity-driven approach.

title: Decentralized Federated Learning with Byzantine Fault Tolerance using Graph Neural Networks
abstract: Federated learning (FL) offers a promising approach to training machine learning models on decentralized data without directly exchanging the data itself. However, FL systems are vulnerable to Byzantine attacks, where malicious participants introduce corrupted data or models to compromise the learning process. This paper proposes a novel decentralized federated learning framework incorporating Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) for Byzantine fault tolerance. The core idea is to represent the federated learning network as a graph, enabling each participant to learn from neighbors while simultaneously detecting and mitigating the influence of potentially malicious nodes. Our approach employs a GNN to learn node embeddings that capture the relationships within the network, allowing for effective identification of Byzantine nodes based on their anomalous behavior. The dynamic, adaptive nature of this system provides a robust defense against Byzantine attacks, enhancing the reliability and trustworthiness of federated learning systems. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework through a theoretical analysis and outline a potential implementation strategy.

abstract: This artifact accompanies the paper “Spectral - Translating Specifications for Deductive Verification into LLVM-IR” which introduces Spectral, a tool that translates specifications from the level of different LLVM based source languages to LLVM-IR. Spectral currently supports specifications for subsets of C, C++ and Swift. This artifact contains the source code of Spectral and the source code of the version of VerCors that has been extended to support Spectral’s specification format. Additionally, the examples that are used in the evaluation of the paper are included. The provided docker image contains executable versions of Spectral and VerCors along with scripts that can be used to replicate the experiments of the paper’s evaluation section (Tables 2 and 3). Additionally, the provided source code of Spectral contains documentation on how to build, use and extend Spectral.

title: Connecting Score Matching, Maximum Likelihood, and Expectation-Maximization in Mixed Linear Regression
abstract: We study variance-preserving diffusion of the response in mixed linear regression (MLR) with unknown mixing weights. Our analysis separates the statistical guarantees of score matching from the loss geometry and optimization signal at a fixed diffusion noise level. The KL divergence links the denoising score matching objective integrated over the diffusion path with the likelihood and a terminal discrepancy. Under mild regularity conditions and terminal schedule, the resulting estimator converges up to the ground truth parameters of MLR, and its scaled error converges to the Gaussian limit of the maximum-likelihood estimator. At a fixed scale of the diffusion noise level, we derive a decomposition linking the score matching loss to cross-entropy and Expectation-Maximization (EM) operators. This decomposition yields an EM-related low-noise gradient expansion with additional correction terms of latent variance. In the high-noise limit, we further characterize gradient descent on this limiting loss under isotropic covariance. Along fixed high signal-to-noise ratio rays, the score matching imbalance gradient and the latent-variance term tend to zero pointwise. Numerical experiments illustrate our theoretical findings and statistical guarantees.

title: Phase Transition Frequency as a Training Time Predictor of Test Accuracy in ResNets
abstract: The number of discrete class-separability jumps observed during ResNet finetuning is examined empirically as a predictor of final test accuracy. Across 75 experiments spanning four benchmarks (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, TinyImageNet, and CIFAR-10-C) and three architectures (ResNet-18, ResNet-50, and ResNet-101), with five to ten seeds per configuration, a strong within-dataset negative correlation is obtained on standard i.i.d. classification benchmarks: \(r = -0.84\) on CIFAR-10 (\(p < 10^{-8}\), \(n = 30\)) and \(r = -0.87\) on CIFAR-100 (\(p < 10^{-5}\), \(n = 15\)). Under distributional stress, the relationship attenuates: TinyImageNet yields \(r = -0.45\), and the CIFAR-10-C corruption benchmark yields \(r = -0.19\). Two additional analyses discipline the empirical claim. A partial correlation controlling for architecture depth, treated as a linear covariate, shows that on CIFAR-100 the transition count retains statistically significant predictive power (\(r_{\mathrm{partial}} = -0.69\), \(p = 0.007\)); the corresponding result under the stricter categorical conditioning is not established at \(n = 15\). A comparison against six alternative training-curve signals shows that transition count achieved the strongest correlation among the evaluated signals on CIFAR-100 and one of the strongest on CIFAR-10, but is dominated by other signals on the two stressed benchmarks. The comparison is restricted to training-curve-level signals; comparisons against effective rank, Hessian sharpness, Fisher information, margin, and neural-collapse measures, which are the strongest competitors in the current literature, are not part of the present study and remain open. The observation is presented as an in-distribution training-quality probe among a family of candidate probes, and an inexpensive detection procedure suitable for logging alongside a standard training loop is provided.

title: Leveraging Low-Level Symbolic Competences for Unsupervised Grounding in Hallucination Detection
abstract: Hallucination-where a language model generates outputs that are factually incorrect or unsupported by the source-is a major challenge for both prompted and fine-tuned language models. Detecting hallucinations is difficult due to the opaque reasoning processes of LLMs, which often provide little insight into why a model's output may be inaccurate. In this work, we investigate whether an LLM can use an alternative, low level, symbolic competence such as SQL for unsupervised hallucination detection in some high level task. For this, we make an LLM build an SQL database from reference documents. This SQL database is then used for reasoning over the reference and the sampled response in a hallucination detection pipeline that is grounded in the database, thereby providing a neurosymbolic checkup. On RAGTruth and DiaHalu hallucination detection datasets, we find that our approach improves on direct prediction and competes with state-of-the-art hallucination detection methods, while not requiring domain-specific fine-tuning. Instead it relies on a low-level general competence already present in LLMs. This warrants further investigation of low-level LLM competences in neurosymbolic approaches.

title: The Knowledge Graph and Evolutionary Trajectory of Artificial Intelligence in Educational Robotics: A Bibliometric Analysis (2016 2025)
abstract: This study uses bibliometric analysis, employing CiteSpace and VOSviewer to examine 313 articles indexed in the Web of Science Core Collection between 2016 and 2025. It systematically maps the knowledge graph, evolutionary trajectory, and emerging trends in the field of artificial intelligence in educational robotics. The findings reveal a paradigm shift from viewing robots as technological tools to viewing them as social partners, characterized by a three-stage evolution: validation of technical feasibility, integration into educational contexts, and reflection on learner centered values. The knowledge network is fragmented—ten coexisting clusters, three fragmented domains, and a hollow center. A pronounced structural hole exists among the three major domains of technical implementation, educational application, and value-based reflection, with no effective mechanism for translating knowledge between them. Frontier trends are dominated by a technological-supply logic, while terms related to ethical reflection are entirely absent from burst detection analysis, reflecting an institutional lag in which technological maturity outpaces normative development. Based on these findings, the study proposes integrated recommendations for academic communities, policymakers, and technology developers to advance the field toward a fair, humanistic, and sustainable educational future.

title: SARCSenti: A Tone-Marked Yoruba Dataset for Sarcasm Detection and Sentiment Classification
abstract: SARCSenti is a tone-marked Yoruba dataset developed for affective natural language processing, specifically binary sarcasm detection and ternary sentiment classification. The analytical release contains 1,507 Yoruba headline records, annotated for both sarcasm and sentiment. Sarcasm labels are non-sarcastic (0) and sarcastic (1), while sentiment labels are negative (0), neutral (1), and positive (2). The dataset contains 1,334 BBC Yoruba-derived records and 173 Yoruba translations derived from the Misra/Kaggle News Headlines Dataset for Sarcasm Detection. Record-level provenance is provided in the source field. Three records from the original research workbook were excluded from the analytical release because of missing or invalid numeric sentiment labels. SARCSenti was developed as part of research conducted in the Department of Computer Science, Lead City University, Ibadan, Nigeria. The dataset is intended to support research on Yoruba and African low-resource NLP, sarcasm detection, sentiment analysis, affective computing, cross-task learning, and the processing of tonal languages. Yoruba text is provided in UTF-8 and normalized using Unicode NFC. The accompanying README and data dictionary provide information on dataset structure, labels, provenance, and usage. Access to the full-text dataset is restricted because a substantial portion contains source-derived BBC Yoruba headline text for which open redistribution rights have not yet been confirmed. Research access may be considered subject to applicable source terms and copyright restrictions.

title: dcat-us-binding: a generated RDF binding for DCAT-US 3.0, and what it does to validation
abstract: DCAT-US 3.0, the United States federal open data metadata profile, is published as a JSON Schema. The live repository ships no JSON-LD context and no SHACL shapes, so its 115 published example files expand to 76 triples, one predicate and zero DCAT triples, with 38 files producing nothing and one processor error. The binding needed to fix that is already inside the schema and unpublished: 26 of 26 classes carry the RDF class they stand for and 231 of 270 properties carry the RDF property, retained when the profile's SHACL definition was retired. This repository generates a JSON-LD 1.1 context and SHACL shapes from those records and measures what changes. Read through the generated context, and with nothing in the corpus edited, the same 115 files expand to 1,510 triples, 123 predicates and 228 DCAT triples, with zero errors. The result the work turns on concerns validation rather than expansion. The profile's own retired shapes, 3,435 lines and 34 node shapes recovered from history, select no focus nodes over the corpus as published, report no violations and return conformance. Run unchanged over the same corpus once it carries a binding, they select 228 focus nodes and report 287 violations. The shapes were never wrong; they were pointed at a graph that did not exist. Secondary findings, each reproducible: four JSON keys map to two different RDF properties depending on the class, three of them in Document; the Concept and Identifier classes have no bound properties at all despite being the most instantiated objects in the corpus; 22 keys declared with a resource range are published as prose 100 times, producing 98 invented identifiers under faithful expansion; and the deprecated context published elsewhere declares a namespace host that does not resolve and mints the W3C Organization Ontology under w3c.org rather than w3.org. Every figure quoted anywhere in the repository is generated into build/measurements.json by the build and pinned by the test suite, so upstream drift fails a test rather than silently rewriting the report. Every RDF figure is computed twice, by rdflib and by the Open Ontologies engine, and every SHACL figure by pySHACL and the same engine, with disagreements reported rather than resolved in favour of the convenient answer. Three defects found that way, two in Open Ontologies and one in rdflib, ship with reproductions. Accepted for the Practitioners Track of SEMANTiCS 2026, the 22nd International Conference on Semantic Systems, Ghent, 17 September 2026, as a demonstration. This is not a paper and appears in no proceedings. Generator code is MIT. Upstream DCAT-US is a work of the United States Government under CC0 1.0, so the generated artefacts in build/ are dedicated to the public domain under CC0 on the same basis. This repository is not a fork and proposes no change to the upstream one.

title: Dynamic Quantum System Optimization
abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic quantum system optimization framework designed to dynamically adjust quantum system parameters in real-time, optimizing quantum systems for enhanced efficiency and improved results. Traditional optimization methods often rely on static parameter settings, limiting adaptability in dynamic environments. We propose a system-state-driven optimization approach utilizing machine learning to automatically tune quantum system parameters, incorporating continuous monitoring and feedback mechanisms. This framework addresses the limitations of static optimization, offering a robust and adaptable solution for complex quantum system design and control. The core mechanism leverages the inherent dynamics of the quantum system itself to guide parameter adjustments, leading to significant improvements in performance. This research presents a practical implementation and analyzes the benefits of this dynamic approach.

title: 基于自适应的概率场模拟的量子计算
abstract: This paper presents a novel quantum computing framework based on adaptive probability field simulation. Traditional quantum computation often relies on fixed parameters, limiting the potential for optimization. This work introduces a dynamically adjusted probability field, enabling significant efficiency gains in quantum computation. The framework leverages this adaptive property to accelerate quantum algorithms and explore novel computational pathways. The core mechanism centers around the construction of a "self-adaptive quantum computation" utilizing a dynamically evolving probability field. We analyze the impact of this approach on various quantum algorithms, demonstrating substantial improvements in performance and scalability. This paper proposes a robust and adaptable method for quantum computing, offering a pathway towards more efficient and versatile computation.

title: Title: Geometric Topology for Adaptive Neural Network Regularization
abstract: This paper investigates the application of geometric topology to enhance the regularization process within neural networks, aiming to improve generalization performance. Traditional regularization techniques often rely on fixed parameters, leading to suboptimal results, particularly in complex datasets. We propose a novel method, 'Geometric Topology Regularization' (GTR), which dynamically adjusts regularization strength based on a continuously evolving geometric topology of the network's structure. This approach leverages a 'geometric topology metric' to monitor network morphology and adaptively modify regularization parameters, thereby mitigating overfitting and boosting predictive accuracy. The core mechanism involves a feedback loop that analyzes network topology and adjusts regularization to achieve a balance between model complexity and generalization. The investigation employs a series of simulations and preliminary experiments to demonstrate the effectiveness of GTR in improving performance on benchmark datasets.

title: Quantum-Enhanced Iterative Complexity (QICE)
abstract: Quantum-Enhanced Iterative Complexity (QICE) presents a novel approach to optimization, employing quantum annealing to accelerate the discovery and improvement of complex mathematical models. This research focuses on utilizing quantum annealing to overcome the inherent limitations of classical computational methods in solving intricate problems. The core mechanism centers around a combination of quantum annealing and iterative refinement algorithms, enabling a significant expansion of the solution space and ultimately enhancing solution accuracy. QICE offers a fundamentally new paradigm in optimization, capitalizing on quantum mechanics to surpass classical computational capabilities. This paper details the theoretical foundations, experimental implementation, and preliminary results demonstrating the effectiveness of QICE in optimizing challenging mathematical models.

title: Title: Quantum Entanglement Through Non-Locality Network Structure
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a cornerstone of quantum mechanics, exhibits correlations that defy classical explanations. The inherent fragility of this entanglement necessitates robust communication protocols. This research explores a novel network structure designed to maintain entanglement across large-scale, distributed networks, leveraging the non-local nature of the system. We propose a model where entanglement strength is directly linked to the network topology and node proximity, offering a potential pathway for reliable communication in a dynamically evolving quantum environment. This work introduces a framework to quantify and manage the inherent entanglement dynamics within such networks. The core claim is that this network structure demonstrably maintains entanglement across significant distances, offering a pathway toward practical quantum communication.

title: Title: Dynamical Network Regularization with Adaptive Thresholds
abstract: This paper presents a novel dynamical network regularization technique designed to accelerate convergence and improve the performance of deep neural networks. Traditional regularization methods often rely on fixed thresholds, which can be suboptimal for complex architectures. We introduce a dynamically adjusted threshold learning mechanism that adapts the threshold value during training based on the network's output and performance. The core principle is to learn thresholds directly from the data, enabling the network to self-regulate and achieve better convergence. We explore the efficacy of this approach through extensive experiments on a range of network architectures and datasets, demonstrating significant improvements in training speed and model accuracy compared to existing regularization methods. The proposed technique offers a promising path towards more efficient and robust deep learning.

title: Self-Organizing Tensor Networks: Adaptive Optimization for Machine Learning
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to machine learning, utilizing Self-Organizing Tensor Networks (SOTN) to dynamically adjust the structure of tensor networks. Traditional tensor networks often rely on pre-defined architectures, limiting flexibility and hindering optimal performance. Our method proposes an automated network adjustment process driven by the inherent properties of SOTN, enabling adaptive optimization and improved efficiency. This research focuses on a method for establishing a dynamic network topology through a series of iterative adjustments based on input data. The core mechanism involves the intelligent manipulation of node connections, resulting in a more robust and efficient model. The novelty of this work lies in the complete implementation of an adaptive network adjustment framework, offering a significant improvement over static network designs. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through several benchmark datasets, showcasing its ability to achieve superior results compared to existing techniques.

title: Quantum State Dynamics and Adaptive Topology Optimization
abstract: Quantum state dynamics represent a fundamental challenge in quantum computing and communication. Traditional optimization approaches often focus on static topologies, limiting the potential for efficient quantum information processing and transmission. This paper explores a novel dynamic topology optimization method leveraging quantum entanglement to dynamically adjust quantum state topology, offering a significant advancement over existing techniques. We introduce a framework that utilizes entangled states to guide a process of state evolution, resulting in improved fidelity, reduced error rates, and enhanced quantum communication capabilities. The core mechanism revolves around the entanglement-driven manipulation of quantum states, enabling a more flexible and powerful optimization strategy. This work demonstrates the potential of this approach through theoretical analysis and preliminary experimental validation.

evidence.abstract: Quantum state dynamics represent a fundamental challenge in quantum computing and communication. Traditional optimization approaches often focus on static topologies, limiting the potential for efficient quantum information processing and transmission. This paper explores a novel dynamic topology optimization method leveraging quantum entanglement to dynamically adjust quantum state topology, offering a significant advancement over existing techniques. We introduce a framework that utilizes entangled states to guide a process of state evolution, resulting in improved fidelity, reduced error rates, and enhanced quantum communication capabilities. The core mechanism revolves around the entanglement-driven manipulation of quantum states, enabling a more flexible and powerful optimization strategy. This work demonstrates the potential of this approach through theoretical analysis and preliminary experimental validation.

title: #基于多变量可塑性的生物启发式神经网络
abstract: This paper introduces a novel bio-inspired neural network architecture leveraging the principle of multi-variable plasticity, mirroring the adaptive mechanisms observed in biological neurons. Traditional neural networks often struggle with complex, high-dimensional data and exhibit limitations in learning efficiency and generalization. Our approach directly addresses these shortcomings by incorporating a multi-variable plasticity model, allowing for a more nuanced and biologically plausible representation of synaptic adaptation. The core of this network utilizes a system where multiple variables associated with a connection (e.g., pre-synaptic activity, post-synaptic potential, time) contribute to the plasticity rule. This is represented by the following equation: ΔWij = η * f(si, sj, t, Rij) where: * ΔWij represents the change in weight between neuron *i* and neuron *j*. * η is the learning rate. * f is the plasticity function, a non-linear function dependent on the input variables. * si is the pre-synaptic firing rate of neuron *i*. * sj is the post-synaptic potential of neuron *j*. * t is the time elapsed since the last spike. * Rij is a regulatory term, representing external influences or feedback. The network's architecture is designed to facilitate this multi-variable plasticity, improving learning speed and overall performance. We demonstrate through a theoretical analysis and simulations that this approach offers superior performance compared to standard single-variable plasticity models, particularly in scenarios involving noisy or complex data. The key innovation lies in the ability to model the complex, interconnected nature of biological synapses and their responsiveness to a variety of stimuli. Future work will explore the network's application in tasks requiring robust adaptation and pattern recognition. ---

title: Based on Topological Dynamics: An Adaptive Neural Network Architecture
abstract: This paper proposes a novel neural network architecture, termed Topological Dynamic Adaptive Network (TDAN), designed to enhance robustness and learning efficiency by mimicking the dynamic topological changes observed in biological neural networks. The core claim is that incorporating these dynamic topological adjustments, specifically through the manipulation of connection weights and neuron activation patterns, can significantly improve the network's ability to handle complex data and generalize to unseen scenarios. The proposed architecture features a mechanism for dynamically adjusting neuron connectivity strength, introducing and eliminating neurons, and facilitating the self-organization of neural groups. Unlike existing adaptive neural networks that primarily focus on weight adjustments, TDAN addresses a critical gap in the field by explicitly modeling the dynamic evolution of the network's internal topology. This approach leverages the inherent resilience and adaptability found in biological systems, potentially leading to more powerful and efficient artificial neural networks.

title: Probabilistic Programming for Embodied AI Reasoning
abstract: Embodied AI systems necessitate reasoning about the physical world to effectively interact and achieve goals. Traditional probabilistic programming languages often fall short in seamlessly integrating sensory data, action execution, and the complexities of dynamic environments. This paper introduces a novel language extension designed specifically for embodied AI, offering a streamlined approach to continuous probabilistic inference over robot states and actions. The core innovation lies in a dedicated syntax and runtime system that directly simulates robot actions, incorporating sensor readings, motor commands, and physics simulations within a unified probabilistic framework. This approach eliminates the need for disjointed simulations and allows for a more holistic understanding of the embodied agent's decision-making process. The proposed system facilitates the development of more robust and adaptable embodied AI agents capable of handling the inherent uncertainties and dynamic nature of the real world. We demonstrate the potential through a conceptual framework and highlight key design considerations.

title: Probability Geometric Neural Networks (PGN)
abstract: This paper introduces Probability Geometric Neural Networks (PGN), a novel deep learning architecture designed to learn complex non-linear functions and exhibit improved generalization and robustness compared to traditional neural networks. The core innovation of PGN lies in its implementation of a probabilistic parameter learning mechanism based on the principles of probability geometry, which allows the model to implicitly learn a set of parameters that are adapted to the data distribution. We present a series of experiments demonstrating the superior performance of PGN across a range of tasks, highlighting its ability to capture intricate relationships and handle noisy data effectively. The paper concludes with a discussion of the theoretical implications of the proposed mechanism and potential future research directions.

title: Dynamic Adaptive Machine Learning Framework
abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic adaptive machine learning framework designed to enhance model generalization by dynamically adjusting model architecture and hyperparameters based on data characteristics and model performance. The framework employs an adaptive algorithm that continuously evaluates model performance and adjusts the architecture and hyperparameters to optimize the model's accuracy and robustness. The core mechanism involves iterative optimization, ensuring the model adapts effectively to evolving data. This research addresses the limitations of static machine learning models by providing a flexible and automated approach to model refinement. We demonstrate the framework's effectiveness through extensive experiments on diverse datasets, showcasing significant improvements in performance compared to traditional approaches.

title: Design and implementation of a SNA-PID controller based on RFNNI applied for the Ball and Beam System
abstract: This paper proposes an adaptive control approach for the ball and beam system using a Single Neuron Adaptive PID (SNA-PID) controller integrated with a Recurrent Fuzzy Neural Network Identifier (RFNNI). The main contribution of this study is the development of an online identification and parameter adaptation scheme, in which the RFNNI is employed to identify the nonlinear system dynamics and provide real-time Jacobian estimation, while the SNA-PID controller updates its parameters online to improve tracking accuracy and robustness against uncertainties. The combination of the single-neuron adaptive structure and the recurrent fuzzy neural network enables effective compensation for nonlinearities and dynamic variations of the system. The proposed control framework is first validated through MATLAB/Simulink simulations and subsequently implemented in real-time experiments with online parameter updating. The experimental setup is based on a DSP control platform and utilizes an infrared (IR) sensor for real-time measurement of ball position. Comparative simulation and experimental results demonstrate that the proposed SNA-PID-RFNNI scheme significantly outperforms the conventional PID controller, achieving a reduction in overshoot from 44.26% to 6.28% and a decrease in settling time from 23 s to 17 s. These results confirm the effectiveness and practical applicability of the proposed adaptive control strategy.
